image021
WINDSOR CASTLE.

MARY BURTON AT WINDSOR.

WINDSOR, Sept. 18—.                 

   "MY DARLING LOLLIE,—Oh! Oh! Lollie dear, how shall I 'begin' to tell you all I have seen to-day. I ought to be tired enough to be in bed and asleep, but you see I am so eager to talk to you that I cannot sleep. Just think! I have been at the Castle all the morning. It has been a perfect day from the first opening of my eyes. We came from London this morning. (That reminds me that I haven't told you a bit about that great beautiful awful city; but we are going back there, and you needn't be afraid; I know I shall write a whole volume about it yet.)

   "Well, Windsor, you know, is only about twenty miles, perhaps not quite that from London, so it took us about an hour to get here. This is Friday, the last day of admittance to the Castle; that is for this week, and it seemed an age to wait for another week, so we just left everything in London and came on to-day. Oh Lollie! How Professor Sargent would criticise that sentence! Wouldn't he? I fancy I can hear him saying,—'Do you think anything in London will suffer very materially because of your absence, Miss Mary?'

   "Well, the Castle; we reached there at a quarter past ten and had to waste an hour, because eleven o'clock is the earliest hour of admittance. Still, of course, there were lovely grounds to look at. Lollie, think of walking through a real castle that has been lived in by kings and queens for so many years. I was half wild with delight. We couldn't see the private apartments at all; they are hardly ever open to visitors. Isn't it mean? What hurt would it do just to let us peep in, and see what their real home rooms look like? It never seems to me as though they had any home, or that they ate, and slept, and laughed and talked like other people. It seems as though they did everything by rule. Lollie, there are thirteen towers in the Castle. The great elegant ball-room and the state dining-room are in these towers. Oh, there are ever and ever so many different buildings, you know; the principal part of the Castle is built in a sort of Court, and there is a lovely round tower in the centre. That is where the governor lives. The top of the tower is more than two hundred feet above the Thames, and the most lovely views of the river can be seen from it. It was rather cloudy to-day, but one of our party said that in fine weather as many as twelve counties could be seen from the tower.

   "Oh, Lollie, if you 'could' see the paintings! Many of them were done by those old artists that we have read stories about. And then some are by artists who are living now. I like the modern ones a little the best, but I suppose that is because I am not capable of understanding the beautiful work of the old masters. Some of our party just raved over paintings that I couldn't see any beauty in. While they were gazing, I took a promenade down the corridor. How long do you suppose it is? Do you remember the academy piazza which was sixty feet long and seemed such a pleasant walk to us? Well, this corridor is five hundred and twenty feet long. I paced back and forth and imagined I saw queen Victoria and the princes and princesses, and all the grand lords and ladies. In fact,—now Lollie, you needn't laugh at me,—I imagined I was one of them myself, and that I wore a white satin dress, and diamonds in my hair and on my neck, and oh, everywhere! It was real fun; ever so much nicer than to be a true princess, because when I got tired of it, I put the white satin and everything out of the way without any trouble and went down into the garden; you go down from the terrace down a long flight of steps, and it is just perfectly lovely there.

   "I can't describe gardens, can you? Oh, Stacey Livermore is here; he went with us to the Castle. We went down the gardens together, and saw Herne's oak. 'Do you know about Herne's oak?' I asked him, and he said, 'Poh, no; I don't know about any of these things. A fellow ought to stay at home and study a hundred years before he comes to Europe. I know that old fellow Shakespeare wrote something about it, but I haven't an idea what.' I didn't know any more about it than Stacey, but I shouldn't wonder if you did. We went the 'Long Walk,' which is a lovely, lovely avenue, three miles long, in the midst of a great, magnificent park. There is a row of old elm trees all the way on each side of the walk. We saw Prince Albert's tomb in the distance. I asked how much it cost, but nobody knew.

   "That reminds me, though, that I 'did' hear what the new stables and riding house cost,—seventy thousand pounds! Think of that! Oh Lollie, I can't tell you about Windsor Castle at all; when I commenced, I thought I could; but there are some things you can't describe.

   "On Monday we are going to Stoke Pogis, (isn't that a horrid name?) Stacey says he knows a lot of things about that place. He is going with us, and he says he'll help me remember things to tell you. He is improved a little I guess,—you know there is room for it. He is different some way; I can't quite make out what it is, but I like him more than I used; he can be real sensible sometimes.

   "Well, dear, I'll try to tell you all about Stoke Pogis."

"It was the awfulest work," giggled Mary.

She had come back from Windsor, and was seated on the doorstep with Lollie who had come for her after supper walk, and to get the foreign mail.

"You see I can't find out much about Windsor Castle. I found a picture of it, and just little bits of description here and there; everything I've said is true, but it made me cross to think how many real nice things I could have told you if I had only known what books to find them in, and then could have got the books. I'll tell you what it is, I mean to find out about it all; somebody knows things of course, and I'll ask questions until I find out. Then I shouldn't wonder if I'd run down to Windsor again, some day, and write you another letter."

"So all you wrote, is strictly true, is it?" asked her friend. "That about Stacey is then, of course?"

Then the two girls looked into each other's eyes, and shouted with laughter.

"I don't care," said Mary at last, "He needs improving, and if I can't do it any other way, I'll do it on paper."

"Are you sure there is no other way, Mary, dear?" Lollie asked her, quietly. "If Stacey were only a Christian, he would be wonderfully improved. Seems to me I would try to help him in something besides Algebra, if I were you."

══════════

FISHING.

NOW, I suppose you think you know all about it, but did you ever swing out of a boat, down a line, into the ocean, as the men in the picture are doing? Let me tell you about it: these men are not working for fish, but for pearls. Do you know what pearls are made of? Nothing in the world but two kinds of lime called "carbonate" and "phosphate" put together with some sticky substance; yet the work is so wonderful that no man has ever found out how to make the lovely balls of light. Jewelers have tried very hard, and made some pretty good imitations, but the strange, quivering sort of shine that the true pearl always has, they can never copy.

Pearls are found, you know, in oyster-shells, but a little grain of sand, or bit of shell, so tiny that it cannot be seen by your or my eye, is always the starting point of each pearl. Around this, the two kinds of lime gather bit by bit, the great artist, who alone can make them, letting them fasten together by the laws which he has made, and by and by there is a brilliant pearl! They are by no means plenty. Sometimes the pearl-divers have to work long before they find one.

image022

Away off in the strait of Manar, near the island of Ceylon, is the place where many of the pearl-oysters are caught. Now for the way they are caught. Here is a picture of the boat. Twenty men belong to each boat; half of them divers, the others, sailors. The boats start out about ten o'clock at night, sail along all night, and reach the fishing-banks about daylight.

They fasten a large stone to a rope, then the diver puts the rope between the toes of his right foot, and slips down under water, the divers above holding on to the other end of the rope. You notice how straight the man going down keeps his head; he is very careful not to go under water head first. With his right hand, he holds on to the rope, and with his left foot, he holds the net into which his oysters are to be put. Now what do you suppose he does with his left hand? Why, holds his nose so that the water cannot get in! Before going down, he takes care to fill his ears with cotton dipped in oil, so that the water cannot fill them. Now he is ready for work. As soon as he reaches the bottom, he picks up every oyster within reach, as fast as he can, fills his bag, hangs it around his neck, gives the signal, grasps the rope again, and is drawn up. He cannot stay under water more than half a minute at a time, and so of course he has to work very fast. Sometimes a diver will make as many as twenty trips under water, for one morning's work, and get not a single pearl! There are only about thirty days in the year in which he can work at his business, but even this, is more than his body can endure. It is such hard and dangerous work that it is said no diver lives to be old, and he is likely to have a very painful and loathsome disease. Besides, there is always danger that a great shark will come while he is picking up oysters, and swallow him.

Is it not strange that any men can be found who are willing to take so much risk and trouble for the sake of earning a little money, or finding a few pearls! Did you ever read about the "pearl of great price?" Did you ever think how strange it was that there are people who will take such trouble to get the "little" pearls that God has made and buried in the ocean, and will not accept this "pearl of great price" from God, as a free gift?

══════════

NEARCHUS.

"WHAT does that word mean?" Claire asked, leaning her elbow on the table, and spelling out the word carefully. Claire was always asking questions.

"Mercy knows! I don't!" This was the way her fifteen year old sister Alice answered.

Then Claire tried again.

"Aunt Margaret, what does Nearchus mean?"

"My name is not Mercy," said Aunt Margaret, "but I think I can answer your question. Nearchus is the name of a man who lived about three hundred and fifty years before Christ came, he was a Greek, and lived in Crete."

"Aunt Margaret, what did he do that made them put him in a book?"

"Oh, well, for one thing he was considered in his day a great traveler. Alexander the Great was very anxious to know about the coast of Asia; he wanted to make a road through the water, from Egypt to India, and sent Nearchus out in command of thirty or forty vessels and two thousand men. It was a long and dangerous voyage for those times, and took a brave man to command. Poor Nearchus had a hard time of it. Great storms came up and hindered, so that when they had been at sea forty days, they had hardly gone eighty miles. Then their provisions almost gave out, and they thought they should certainly starve. The emperor sent a ship after them with provisions, and they tried again; they had a shipwreck, losing two or three of their vessels; they came across wild people on the islands, who tried to make war with them; and, indeed, you can hardly think of anything wild and ugly that did not happen to them while they were gone."

image023

"But, auntie, what is going on in this picture? I don't see any natives here."

"Let me see! Oh, these are worse than natives, they are whales! Nearchus, when he sailed into the Persian gulf, came across a great army of them. The sailors were dreadfully frightened, the whales were so large, and there were so many of them. At first, Nearchus thought he would have to turn back, the sailors were so afraid, but finally he succeeded in putting some of his own courage into their hearts, and they made a brave fight, and scattered the whales.

"On they went, and soon they came across lovely shores, where were fruit trees of almost every kind, and corn-fields, and pasture-land. I think they must have had a very good time after that; still they didn't know as much as they thought they did, for all the while they were sailing up the Persian gulf, they thought it was the Red sea. They stopped at a little island that is now called Ormuz, after having been more than six months on the water. There they heard good news. Alexander and his army were only five days' march from them. You may be sure they started on that march as fast as they could. It is said that Nearchus' trials and hardships had changed him so that Alexander did not know him. The fleet had been so long unheard from, that it was given up for lost. So they offered sacrifices to the gods in gratitude for his safe return. He came back home with great honors, and was feasted and admired."

"But, after all, did his journey do any good?"

"Why, yes dear, a little; he gave his mite to the knowledge of the country. I suppose we know a bit more about the world to-day, than we would have known if Nearchus had stayed at home."

Claire sighed, and said with a thoughtful face, "Folks have to take lots of trouble to know things."

"No," said her sister, laughing; "I don't think you do; you just have to pour out questions to Aunt Margaret, and she answers them all."

Silence for a few minutes, and then another question—"Aunt Margaret, where is Nearchus now?"

"What a child!" said Alice.

And Aunt Margaret with a very grave face answered—

"You know he has been dead more than eighteen hundred years, Claire; and yet he is living! God is the only one who knows about him now."

Claire gave another little sigh, and said pitifully—

"I wish he had lived until Jesus Christ was born, and he would have told him it was no good to ask Jupiter and those foolish gods to take care of him."

"But perhaps, dear, he would not have given his love and service to Jesus even then; some people who know about him, do not, you know."

This made sister Alice blush, but she said not a word.

image024

MARY BURTON AT STRATFORD-ON-AVON.

   "DEAR LOLLIE,—Isn't it queer for me to be spending more than half a day in an 'old' church! Some of our party just wanted to keep staying and 'staying!' But then I didn't wonder; 'you' would have liked it, Lollie. Of course, you know the church at Stratford-on-Avon is the place where Shakespeare is buried—though I didn't know it until Mr. Burnham told me so. If it were not for that same Mr. Burnham, I should know very little about the places where we go. But he comes up and answers all my questions, besides a great many that I want to ask, and don't like to."

image025
INTERIOR OF CHURCH AT STRATFORD-ON-AVON.

   "We saw the house where he used to live,—Shakespeare I mean, not Mr. Burnham; and now I think of it, I don't mean even that, for the house was pulled down, but somebody has built another just like the old one, so we can see what it was. A common enough house; I think I like ours at home, better. Still it seemed strange to walk around it, and think what a great man once lived in it; and people didn't know he was going to be a great man! I suppose his father punished him, and his mother boxed his ears, occasionally, just as though he was not going to be the greatest poet in the world! I stood looking at the great slab lying in the chancel, and by the way, it has a horrid verse on it. I copied it for you, spelling and all—

"'GOOD FREND FOR IESVS SAKE FORBEARE
  TO DIGG THE DVST ENCLOASED HEARE.
  BLEST BE YE MAN YT SPARES THESE STONES,
  AND CVRST BE HE YT MOVES MY BONES.'

   "I asked Mr. Burnham if it was supposed that Shakespeare wrote those lines, and he said, he believed some people supposed so, but it would be hard to prove it, or make scholars believe it. Then he asked me why I looked so dissatisfied; wasn't Shakespeare's tomb satisfactory? I laughed, and said, that I wanted to know a hundred things. He told me to ask him fifty of them, and see if he could answer. 'Well,' I said, 'I don't know anything about Shakespeare before he became famous. I want to know what kind of a boy he was,—rich or poor, a good scholar, or bad, and everything.' 'Poor,' he said. 'His father was once quite wealthy, but when William was about fourteen, he had to leave school and go to work, earning his own living.'

   "'What did he do?' I asked, eagerly, and I wondered if even as early as that, he wrote verses that people paid money for. But what do you think was my answer!

   "'Well, it is supposed, and with very good reason, that he became a butcher.' Think of it, Lollie, the great Shakespeare a 'butcher!' Then Mr. Burnham said it was thought that he also taught school for a time, but nothing was very certain about this part of his life. You see, the trouble was, they didn't know he was going to be famous, and so took no pains to remember about his boyhood. But before he was nineteen, he married! His wife's name was Anne Hathaway, and she was about twenty-seven when they married! I don't think he was very good to her; only think! all he left her in his will was a bed! It doesn't seem to me, from all I have heard, that he was a very good man, if he 'was' a great one; but Mr. Burnham says he was better than many men, in his time. His monument is horrid! At least I think so: a great awful 'skull' on the top! The little angels on each side are sort of ugly-looking creatures, too. I don't like the great man's face, either; this is what it says both in Latin and English, on his monument, 'In judgment a Nestor, in genius a Socrates, in art a Virgil; the earth covers him, the people mourn him, heaven possesses him.' I asked Mr. Burnham if he were a good man,—that, is a Christian,—and he said he had never heard anything that would lead him to think so. Then I don't think they ought to put that last sentence on his monument, do you?"

image026
SHAKESPEARE'S TOMB.

   "He was just fifty-three years old when he died, in April, 1616. How almost 'awful' it seems to think of any one having been dead for more than two hundred and fifty years!

   "Lollie, do you know much about Shakespeare's writings? I told Mr. Burnham that I didn't believe I had ever read a dozen lines that he wrote; and he answered, that there was time enough for me to read him, if I lived; but he thought quite likely I had a great many lines of his without knowing it, as he was more often quoted than almost any other author. 'But,' he added, 'I would rather have Bunyan's monument.' I didn't know anything about Bunyan's monument, and I told him so. And he promised when we went to see it, to tell me a great deal about it, and him.

   "Then he read for me Anne Hathaway's epitaph written by her son. It is in Latin; I made a copy it: 'My mother, thou gavest me milk and life; alas for me that I can but repay thee with a sepulchre! Would that some good angel might roll the stone away and thy form come forth in the Saviour's likeness! But my prayers avail not. Come quickly, O Christ! then shall my mother, though enclosed in the tomb, arise and mount to heaven.' I liked that epitaph best, because it sounded as though somebody loved her.

   "Lollie, I had a feeling, standing by those graves that had been there for two hundred and fifty years, that nothing lasted but 'graves!' I said something like it to Mr. Burnham, and he smiled, and said, I must not forget my own soul which was to last after those marbles had crumbled into dust. I'm going to write about something pleasant, next time, I guess.

"Your loving,

"MARY."

══════════

KARL THE SMALL.

HE wailed over his writing-book. He hated writing, he declared, and wished that the man who invented it had never been born. His copy-book was filled with huge mountains and dark valleys of ink; he had forgotten how to make a capital Z, and he never knew how to make a capital K, and he couldn't tell b from d, and O, he had a dreadful time! Perhaps worse than all was the fact that his beloved teacher said his writing looked like "hens and chickens walking over a marsh!" He laid his arms on the table, and his head on his arms, and cried outright.

"I declare!" said his big brother. "If he isn't like his namesake, Karl the Great! I wonder in how many other things he resembles him?"

This sounded as though there might be a story coaxed out of the big brother, and Karl the Small was always ready for stories. He took his head from the table and asked one question, "Who was he?"

"Your namesake. Why, he was a good old German king who lived about a thousand years ago. A good fellow he was, too, a brave soldier, and one who tried to be sure that he was fighting for the right. Here is a picture of him; see what a fine-looking man he was."

image027

And the big brother took down a book from the library and turned the leaves, and young Karl leaned his elbows on the table again and stared at his namesake.

"Who is that man he is shaking hands with?"

image028

"That is Witikind, one of his conquered enemies; a brave soldier, too, who was determined that he 'wouldn't' be conquered, but he was. He was a heathen, and fought for his idol god, but when Karl conquered him, he gave up his idols and became a Christian. Your namesake used to have some fine presents sent to him; among them came one day, an elephant."

"My!" said young Karl, his eyes sparkling.

"You would have liked that. But I believe I would rather have had his clock."

"What kind of a clock?"

"Well, the name of it was a 'water clock;' every hour a bright ball would drop into a brass bowl, and a handsome little knight all fixed up, would come out at one o'clock and march around; at two o'clock two knights would appear, and so on."

Young Karl declared the clock to be splendid, but still believed he should like the elephant. Silence for a few moments while the boy stared at his namesake. Then he ventured another question: "How am 'I' like him?"

"Why," said the big brother, laughing, "though he could read and speak Latin, beautifully, it is said he could never learn to write! But I'll tell you one thing, my boy, he 'tried' hard; carried his tablets about with him, and practised whenever he had a chance; but he had so many cares, the chances were rare. It is my opinion if he had done as his namesake is doing—learned when he was a little boy—he would have been all right."

"I mean to study German," said young Karl, thoughtfully.

══════════

WHAT LUCIUS KNEW.

"NOW for it! One, two, three, run!"

And away went the three boys, from the top of Burr's hill; a grand race for life, or for fame; it was to be decided who could first reach the meadow gate, a quarter of a mile away—the two brothers, or Lucius, the cousin from the country, who was visiting them. He was a swift runner; he gained on them every minute, and I think would have reached the gate first, if any of them had reached it first, or indeed at all. But an unlucky root of a gnarled old tree poking itself above ground in the way, caught Lucius' foot at just the wrong minute, and down he went, rolling over and over like a ball.

The cousins came up panting and breathless, to stop the ball, and find out the bruises. But Lucius shook himself, and declared that he was not hurt, and could tear that old root up with his teeth to pay it for stopping the race.

"History repeats itself," quoted Cousin Will, laughing. "Brutus has been kissing his mother."

"What do you mean?" asked Lucius, opening his eyes very wide.

"Why, you know about Lucius Junius Brutus?" said Will, dropping on the grass to rest himself.

"No, I don't," said Lucius, dropping down beside him, while Harry strolled off to search for ferns. "What about him?"

"Oh, he went with his cousins to see the Delphic Oracle; those old Rooms were always asking their 'Oracle' what was going to happen, you know. Well, Junius Brutus was supposed to be, not very bright, but that was all put on, because he was a little afraid of his cousins. They asked the Oracle, the brothers did, you know, who would be the ruler of Rome after their father died; and she said the one who kissed his mother first, after they reached home. Well, the brothers had an older brother named Sextus, and they agreed to keep still about this to him. They made for home, each bent on being the first to kiss the mother, but just as they were setting foot in the city of Rome, down tumbled Lucius Junius Brutus, making believe fall, you see, and 'kissed' the ground. He was the only one who had understood the Oracle to mean by the word 'mother' the earth out of which we are all made."

Lucius laughed. "He was a sharp fellow to understand what the Oracle meant," he said. And then, after a moment he added, "I wish 'I' knew things as you and Harry do."

"Study history, my man, and then you will know 'some' things."

"Kissing his 'mother,'" Lucius said, musingly; "yes, that is true; 'Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.'" Then, after a moment of silence, "But I know a thing worth forty of that. I wonder if 'you' do?"

"What is it?"

"Why, do you know what Job said?"

"Job! Let me see, he was that old fellow who had so much trouble, and grumbled, or no—he didn't grumble, did he? What about him?"

"He said, 'I know that my Redeemer liveth, and though after my skin, worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God.' I know he is 'my Redeemer,' too."

Then they were still for as much as five minutes; and when Will spoke again, his voice was low and grave. "Then old fellow, you know more than either of us."

══════════

SEXTUS TARQUINIUS.

HE was a famous Roman. Among other ways in which he won fame, he deceived a whole army. There was war between his country and another. Sextus pretended to run away from his father, came to the enemy, told them he had been badly treated by his father, and had deserted. They believed his story, took him in, trusted him. And in course of time, he had command of the army and the city. Then he sent to his father for instructions, as to what to do.

It is said that the father was walking through a field when his son's message arrived. He chose not to put his answer into words, for fear, I suppose, that some harm might come to him in the future, because of them. So, without speaking a word, he switched off the heads of all the poppies that were growing around him. Then he told the messenger to tell Sextus what he had seen.

Back went the man with his strange message. But Sextus understood it at once. He managed so as to have all the chief men in the enemy's army, put to death. Then the Romans marched in and took the city.

Wouldn't it be a sad thing to live a long life, and be remembered at last only for some deed of cruelty, or selfishness, or cowardice? I wonder, whether two thousand years from now, people will be reading about some of the Pansy boys and girls, as we are reading now about Sextus, and his father, Tarquin? If so, I wonder what will be remembered of you?

HOW A CITIZEN BECAME A SOLDIER.

ONE day I was walking through the streets of York, in England. I saw a little way ahead, a soldier coming toward me. He had the red uniform on of the infantry—the dress of the army. I knew at once when I saw him that he was a soldier.

When he came near me, I stopped him. I said, "My good man, if you have no objections, I would like to ask you a few questions."

"Certainly, sir," said he.

"Well, then, I would like to know how you first became a soldier?"

"Yes, sir, I will tell you. You see, sir, I wanted to become a soldier, and the recruiting officer was in our town, and I went up to him and told him I wanted to enlist.

"'Well, sir,' he said, 'all right.'

"And the first thing he did, sir, he took an English shilling out of his pocket, sir, and put it into my hand. The very moment, sir, a recruiting-sergeant puts a shilling into your hand, sir, you are a soldier."

I said to myself, "That is the very illustration I want."

That man was a free man at one time—he could go here and there, do just what he liked, but the moment the shilling was put into his hand, he was subject to the rules of war, and Queen Victoria could send him anywhere and make him obey the rules and regulations of the army. He is a soldier the very minute he takes the shilling. He has not got to wait to put on the uniform. And when you ask me how a man may be converted at once, I answer, just the same as that man became a soldier. The citizen becomes a soldier in a minute, and from being a free man becomes subject to the command of others. The moment you take Christ into your heart, that moment your name is written in the roll of heaven.

EARLY LOVE TO CHRIST.

A little girl was desirous of publicly professing her faith in Christ.

One of the elders said to her, "When do you think you commenced to love the Lord Jesus?"

"I don't know, sir; but I think it was when I began to love my mother."

LOUISE IN GERMANY.

"OH! Ho! Hum," yawned Rufus, and he stretched himself on the sofa at full length, and then yawned again.

Presently he spoke, "I say, Louise, have you got your lesson? I don't 'begin' to know mine; it's an awful lesson."

Louise was in one of the easy chairs, book in hand, an amused smile on her face, and she laughed outright as her brother spoke.

"Almost," she said, in answer to his question. "What a queer man the Emperor Joseph was?"

"Queer? I don't know. Why?"

"Oh, I think it was fun to travel as he did, not let people know who he was, and surprise them."

This sounded to seven-year-old Stevie like a story, so he left his blocks and came and hung on his sister's chair.

"How could he do it?" he asked her.

"Oh, he dressed in plain clothes, and rode on alone, without his suite; he stopped at common-looking hotels and ate sausages for dinner; once he offered to be the godfather of a child who lived in a dreadful little hut. They seemed to like him, and decided that he should be their child's godfather, if he would come the next day. So he came; but it was in his elegant dress, with his sword flashing by his side, and the emperor's crown on his head.

"Another time he took supper with a very poor man who had ten children of his own, but who had adopted a poor orphan. They didn't know they were eating supper with the emperor, and they did not find it out until the next day when he sent a present of a good deal of money, to each of the eleven children.

"I should have just enjoyed doing such things; it must have been real fun. Still, he wasn't very happy; he tried to make better laws, but the people didn't like them; and I guess he was better at planning than at doing, for he said himself they ought to put over his grave, 'Here lies a man who, with the best intentions, never carried out a single plan.'"

"Look here, Louise," said Rufus, rising on one elbow, "where did you find all that?"

"Why, in our history lesson, of course."

"'I' haven't seen a word of it."

"Why, Rufus Smythe! Then you haven't 'half' studied your lesson; it is all there."

"It isn't so nice as my lesson," declared Stevie. "Mine is about a man that the people didn't know who he was, and he met a funeral, and he stopped them and spoke to the dead man, and he got right up and was alive and well! Your Emperor Joseph couldn't do that."

"No," said Louise, stooping to kiss Stevie. "Your story is a great deal the nicest; it is about the greatest king who ever lived."

MARY BURTON AT SMITHVILLE.

THAT is not in Europe, you understand; but is the pretty little village where Mary lives. Just at this writing, she is not in the most amiable of moods. She is seated in a low chair, by the west window of Lollie Adams' room, engaged in hemming a ruffle so that Lollie can shirr it.

"So there is no foreign mail, to-day?" questioned Lollie, a shadow of a smile hovering around her lips, she sewing, meanwhile, very fast.

"No, there isn't, and I'm out of all patience; I meant to have just the nicest letter for you. I saw a picture of Westminster Abbey, and I wanted to write about it; but do you believe, after trying hard for two days, I can't find anything that sounds like real plain English about it. Where is Westminster Abbey, anyhow?"

"More than I know," laughed Lollie, "I am not in Europe, you will remember, and have never been."

"Well, what is it? A church where they have meetings every Sunday, and does the queen go there to church? And what is there so very wonderful in it?"

"I haven't the least idea," said Lollie, serenely.

"That's just it, neither have I; and I've tried as hard as ever a mortal could, to learn. I suppose I haven't the right sort of books, but I wish I could find out what sort to get. I hunted through Uncle Robert's encyclopædia and found just nothing at all. And in one book, I found a sentence that read as though everybody knew all about it, of course, and there was no need to spend any time on it. 'Westminster Abbey is of course too well known to need any description from me,'—that is what one writer said; I find plenty of such sentences. I believe when people don't know anything about a thing, they say that. I'm going to try it. After this, whenever you come to a sentence which tells about things so well known that they may be passed over in silence, you may understand that I don't know the least thing about them, and neither does anybody else that I can find to talk with.

"I asked Stacey Livermore to-day, if he was posted on Westminster Abbey, and he said, 'Why, yes, of course; everybody was. Edward the Confessor had it built, instead of going on a pilgrimage to Rome as he had promised.' But when I began to question him, as to how it looked, and where it was, and what it was for, and the things that had made it famous, he knew no more than a kitten. I spent the whole of last Saturday morning in the library, going over old, musty books, that, judging from their titles, would have something to say about Westminster, and every one of them talked as though of course I knew it all! I tell you what it is, Lollie, I do hope I will really and truly go to Europe some day, so I can write a book, and I'll describe things so plainly that people can see them the minute they shut their eyes."

"I hope you will," said Lollie, laughing, "I 'sincerely' hope you will go, both for your sake and mine. But in the mean time, dear, don't pucker that hem. You need help in the selection of books; why don't you ask Mr. Burnham what to get to read up on Westminster?"

"So I will," declared Mary, with brightening eyes; "that will be just the thing. There, Lollie Adams, you have given me the first real help on Westminster that I've had this week. Oh, I'll know something yet. You shall have your description, see if you don't."

"And about Stacey, is he improving anywhere except on paper, yet?"

"No; he's horrid. He lounges into Sabbath school when it is nearly half out, and knows as little about his lessons as I do about Westminster."

"Perhaps, little girlie, he needs some real out spoken help from you; as much as you need it on another subject. How much do you say to him on this subject, so much more important to understand, than Westminster can be?"

Silence for a few minutes, then Mary said, "Lollie, you are just 'awful' to ask questions. Hand me the scissors, please. I don't know how to help Stacey, but I suppose I might try."

OVER THE SEA.

AWAY off in Italy is a beautiful city named Florence. It is built on either side of the lovely river Arno. It is said to be a city where there is a great deal of sunshine, and a perfect glow of flowers; in fact, its pet name is "The City of Flowers." There are many beautiful buildings, picture galleries, public libraries, and the like, but the one spot where I want to go to-day, is the cemetery where Mrs. Elizabeth Barrett Browning is buried. She, you know, was a poetess. I wonder if you have yet read any of her wonderful poems? She was born in London, seventy-two years ago. It is said that when she was a very young girl she wrote beautiful poems, but she had a wise father, who encouraged her to write only for him, and to study hard. The consequence was, when she began to write for other people, she was so well prepared that they saw she was a genius.

When I was a girl, I read her long poem "Aurora Leigh," and loved it. I selected bits from it for recitation; I remember one, a description of Aurora's fancy work, a maiden in canvass and wools with pink eyes, and blue hair, I think it was, and then occurs these lines—

"We sew, 'sew'! prick our fingers, dull our sight;
 And all for what? A pair of slippers, sir,
 To rest you when you're weary;
 Or a stool, to stumble o'er and vex you."

Mrs. Browning was a good and true woman, as well as a very talented one. Here is a picture of the great marble tomb, resting on six marble columns, which covers the spot where she sleeps. The initial letters of her name and the date of her death, which you see in the picture, are all the lettering there is on the monument.

Now I am going to copy for you a few verses of that one among her poems which the children like best. It is entitled—

"THE ROMANCE OF THE SWAN'S NEST.
 
"Little Ellie sits alone
 'Mid the beeches of a meadow,
 By a streamside, on the grass,
 And the trees are showering down
 Doubles of their leaves in shadow,
 On her shining hair and face.
 
"She has thrown her bonnet by,
 And her feet she has been dipping
 In the shallow water's flow.
 Now she holds them nakedly
 In her hands, all sleek and dripping,
 While she rocketh to and fro.
 
"Little Ellie sits alone,
 And the smile she softly uses,
 Fills the silence like a speech,
 While she thinks what shall be done,—
 And the sweetest pleasure chooses
 For her future within reach."

Oh, I should like to give you the whole story of little Ellie, but there are seventeen verses, and you see I haven't room. It is full of the queer and quaint fancies of that little barefooted girl.

After all, pretty as the poem is, if you and I were standing by that great white marble tomb, thinking and talking; about the sleeper, perhaps we would rather repeat this verse of hers just then, than any other that she wrote.

"Of all the thoughts of God that are
 Borne inward into souls afar.
 Among the Psalmist's music deep.
 Now tell me, if there any is,
 For gift or grace, surpassing this,—
 'He giveth his beloved sleep.'"

CHOP STICKS.

HOW would you like to have only two long thin sticks with which to take up your food and throw it into your mouth? This young Chinaman stands all ready to use his, which he has between his fingers. I suppose there is rice in the bowl. The question is, how is he going to take up rice with those two sticks! There is nothing like knowing how. Oh, I wonder if this boy with his pleasant, intelligent face, knows about the true God, or still prays those foolish senseless prayers, such as the people of his country offer to their idols. A lady who has been a missionary in China for ten years told me that some of the Chinese think they will be rewarded for the number of prayers they say. They have one sentence which they call a prayer; I don't know just what it means, nor do they, but they constantly repeat it. "Oh, Me Toh Fee," that is the sentence, I believe; and my friend says she often has conversations like these: "What kind of a dress is that you wear? Oh, me toh fee." "What makes you Melicans so pale? Oh, me toh fee." "How far is it to where you live? Oh, me toh fee." Think of calling that a prayer! So they try hard to get a great many prayers said through the day. So anxious are they to please their idol in this way that some of them never ask a question, or make a remark, without closing with the words "Oh, me toh fee." Dear me! What an example they are to us after all! How many of us who know how to pray, and who are sure the Saviour hears and answers us, care to please him by speaking to him often? Surely we ought to make haste to teach these Chinese, who are willing and anxious to pray, how to reach the ear of the true God.

WATCH YOUR WORDS.

KEEP a watch on your words, my darlings,
  For words are wonderful things;
They are sweet, like the bees' fresh honey—
  Like the bees, they have terrible stings;
They can bless, like the warm, glad sunshine,
  And brighten a lonely life;
They can cut, in the strife of anger,
  Like an open two-edged knife.
 
Let them pass through your lips unchallenged,
  If their errand is true and kind—
If they come to support the weary,
  To comfort and help the blind;
If a bitter, revengeful spirit
  Prompt the words, let them be unsaid;
They may flash through a brain like lightning,
  Or fall on a heart like lead.
 
Keep them back, if they're cold and cruel,
  Under bar and lock and seal;
The wounds they make, my darlings,
  Are always slow to heal.
May peace guard your lives, and ever,
  From the time of your early youth,
May the words that you daily utter
  Be the words of beautiful truth.

IN THEIR HAPPY CHILDHOOD.

JOHN AND MARY.

MANY years ago there lived in the great city of J— two children, John and Mary. Often they played together, and went hand in hand to school. And many a time, as they were coming home, now looking into a shop window or hurrying by a saloon, or almost pushed from the narrow sidewalk by some drunkard, they promised each other, when they should grow up, that they would fight with "all their might and main" for Temperance. John said, if he could only study law and become a smart man, and get into office, he would close up the rum-shops—he would defend the poor widow and fatherless. And little Mary promised she would never marry a man who drank.

But, like too many boys and girls who promise never to touch or taste strong drink, both of them, when temptation came, forgot their promises. I've known so many strong temperance girls who said they never would keep company with young men who smoked, and went to saloons and theatres and such places, and yet two-thirds of those very same girls, a few years later, did just what they were not going to do. Some of you say you will always keep clear of all this nasty, dreadful business. I wonder if you will. God help you! You can't escape unless you are kept by his mighty power, because you are fighting against "the rulers of the darkness of this world." No one has ever stood against such foes alone. I tremble for you, if you are not on the Lord's side, and he on yours.

But we must follow John and Mary a few years. Both grew up, John becoming so popular he was made a judge; and so he had a good chance to carry out his early promises about temperance. But he cared more for his office, and how he might keep it year after year, than he did to use it for the comfort of the oppressed and as a terror to evil doers. So he soon fell into bad society, spent a good deal of his time gambling and drinking, and became very profane and wicked and hard-hearted. The devil has used alcohol and gaming and such things to make men hate God and each other.

As for Mary, she was soon engaged to be married. It was a most beautiful day in May when, amid the good wishes of friends and the songs of birds, she started on her wedding tour—a beautiful beginning, as most are, but, like most, a sad ending. She is soon a widow, and with an enemy. She married a very nice young man, "except" that he was not a total abstainer. He would not sign the pledge, nor would he promise never to touch strong drink; one of those, you know, who "will not sign away their liberty," who "know what they can stand," who "will not be such fools as to be contemptible drunkards."

For a time, he was a loving and industrious husband. Then he became very intimate with some of the fast young husbands who invited him to their club meetings. There he met the judge, and there drank and gamed.

It is never far from some of those club-houses to the lowest dens. This young husband who "would not sign away his liberty" was not long in finding his way there, and, little by little, his money went into the saloon-keeper's till, while he now could drink glass after glass, with the judge at his side. Finally nothing was left but a craving appetite, a wasted name and home, and wife and children in tears and rags.

Last of all (the old story—you can read it when you will in the dailies), that husband was killed in a drunken carousal in the place where he spent all his earnings—murdered, and cast out-door, like a dog, by the saloon-keeper.

Can you blame that wretched Mary—now a widow, with her homeless, friendless children—if she cried for justice against that cruel adversary?

Ah, how many Marys are now wringing their hands and crying, as they look down into open graves where a once-beloved friend is being lowered, to awake in the great day of judgment to "shame and everlasting contempt"—for it is written over the gateway of heaven, "Drunkards shall not enter"!

What an "adversary," indeed, is strong drink! And how Mary, as she comes from the cemetery to her desolate home, must have thought of her beautiful childhood, and that lovely spring morning when she became a happy bride! And now all was so soon night and winter. And how came it all? Who did it? And what would save her dear boy from the fate of the miserable father? She would go immediately to the judge; he would surely pity her, and aid her in her effort to bind and destroy this adversary.

She was soon on her way. The street was crowded. The throngs jostled her this way and that, but her heart was too sore, and her purpose too grand, to be frightened by anything. So on she presses, right by the dreadful place where her husband spent his last night—right over the walk, stained even now with his blood.

There is the judge, sitting in state—put there to plead the cause of the poor, the widow and fatherless. Down at his very feet, she casts her weary self.

"For God's sake, give me back my home and comforts that my adversary has stolen away; and, if need be, bind him in prison, lest he reach forth and destroy my dear boy also! For the sake of our childhood's days, for the sake of promises made years ago, for the sake of your own sons and daughters, for the sake of hundreds whose hearts are sadder than even mine!"

No wonder he drove her away, and commanded his officers to hush her cries. What could such a man care for Mary's tears and entreaties now? Hadn't he learned to care for neither God nor man, through his love for office and money and strong drink? Maybe that "adversary" was standing near, and whispered to the judge that if he regarded this widow, he would see to it that all the saloon-keepers would vote against him. That was enough. How many unjust judges there are now-a-days! They were once temperance boys, I suppose, many of them; they signed the pledge, and sang temperance songs, and recited temperance verses from the Bible, and we thought they would make grand temperance men in a few years. But, they grew up, and wanted office, and got it—some of them by thinking and "treating," and pledging saloon-men, if they would elect them, they would serve them. And they are doing the bidding of their masters. Thousands of poor, suffering widows come pleading before them, year after year, to make good laws against these wicked rum-sellers, or defend the laws, or execute them. And the long, weary years drag by, and, like this unjust judge, they will not "do justly, and love mercy, and walk humbly," and "relieve the cry of the distressed."

image036
PEACOCK'S COMPLAINT TO JUNO.

But cry on, sorrowing, broken-hearted Marys, against the great adversary, Rum. Even this godless, cruel judge did at last relent before such pleading. Cry on, dear boys and girls, against your great enemy, strong drink. And cry not so much to hard, cruel man for aid, as to our mighty, loving God, who will avenge his own speedily that cry day and night to him, though he bear long with them. Read Luke xviii.

A ROMAN PEASANT.

HASN'T she a pleasant face? If this picture were colored, it would be more striking; a Roman peasant woman's idea of dress seems to be to get as many and as bright colors together as she can. Scarlet and white are favorite colors, especially for head-dresses. The girls are apt to wear short, pink dresses and blue aprons, embroidered richly in all the colors of the rainbow.

image037

One writer, in speaking of the dresses of the baby peasants, said the effect was to make them look like butterflies. Can you imagine a clean-faced, carefully kept baby in anything but a white dress?

I am afraid that this class of peasants in Rome do not bear a very high character. They seem to get their living in doubtful ways, and much of their gayety belongs only to their dress, for I think there must be among them very heavy hearts. They are very different from the peasant women of Holland; these are "workers." Their long, dark woolen stockings, and short, dark woolen dresses look as if made for use instead of show. They have one curious fashion, that is a head-dress made of gold, pure gold at that; it must be about two inches wide, and goes all around the head. A peasant woman seems to feel that whatever comfort or necessity she has to do without, she "must" have a head-dress; the cheapest of them are said to cost forty dollars, while many cost more than a hundred. Only the very poor and miserable wear silver ones; none go without. Did you ever think what a pleasant mark of our religion it was, that women who belong to Jesus Christ have no such trammels of fashion? At least they need not have; He has made us free; neither gold bands, nor silver, nor yet iron ones, need be worn by us. What a strange sight it would be to see a poor, hard-working woman, who had little children to support, paying forty dollars for a gold band to wear around her head. How sure we would be, if she lived in this country, that she had not given her heart to Jesus. I wonder if we, any of us, wear about us, in our dress or on our faces, marks which show that, we have not given ourselves to him?

MARY BURTON IN LONDON.

LONDON, Aug. 18—.                 

   "DEAREST LOLLIE,—You couldn't guess where I have been all the morning: in a meat market! Don't you think I must have been hungry? But really it seems to me just now as though I never 'should' be, again, or want to see any more meat, but I suppose I shall like it as well as ever by to-morrow. Ah! But the market where I have been is well worth going to see. Do you remember Sarah Williams describing to us Fulton Market, in New York? Dear me! I wonder what she would think of London market. Lollie, imagine iron gates twenty-five feet high, nineteen feet wide, and weighing fifteen tons. Nineteen feet wide! Why my room at home is only fourteen feet wide, and you know we think it a pretty good sized bedroom. Three acres of market! 'Can' you imagine it? The roof is made of glass, and fancy iron work, and is just as pretty as it can be. If you can imagine how large a place three acres is, just go up to Mr. Burnham's and walk around the grounds, he says there are just three acres.

   "You may imagine it took us some time to walk through the market, for there were so many things to gaze at, and it is six hundred and thirty feet long. Under the market, there is a railroad depot; tracks are laid from there to all the railroads in London, and even out into the country, so that people can get their meat sent to them at the last minute. One of the waiters told us there was a train passed through their depot every two minutes, all day long. There are one hundred and sixty shops, or stalls, in this market ranged on either side of the avenues. Think of having avenues for promenading through a market. They are just splendid, anyway. The central one is thirty feet wide; then there are six side avenues, each twenty feet wide. Oh, I can't tell you how lovely it was to stand at one end of the main avenue, and look away down as far as the eye could reach; a wide, straight beautiful walk, with lovely glass roof, mixed in with ornamental iron arches and pillars, and great balls of fire, for gas lights.

   "Oh Lollie, I couldn't realize that there were people enough in the world to eat all the meats that we saw in that market. I said something of that sort to Mr. Burnham, and he said that he would like to have everything in it cooked, ready for eating, then open the great gates, and call on those who had no breakfast and no dinner, to come in and eat. 'I don't think by dark there would be a mouthful left,' he said. Only think of it! So many hungry people in London. Oh I saw such queer-shaped eggs, just mountains of them piled up. I could think what they were, but a man told us they were plover's eggs. Then don't you think I saw eagles to 'eat!' They come from Norway, and are not like our American eagles, but still I should think that no American would like to eat them just for the sake of the name.

   "Well, it was a nice, clean, cool, elegant place. Think what an immense amount of money must have been spent on building it, and how much it takes every day to keep it stocked. And there are people enough to eat all the food displayed there, and in hundreds of other places, and still hundreds go hungry; and this is all in one city. What a 'great big world it is!' How 'can' God take care of it all? This evening when we had prayers in our parlor, Mr. Burnham read the verse, 'Not a sparrow falleth to the ground without our Father.' Then he looked directly at me, for I had told him I couldn't realize that God could think of so many people at once. Oh I was glad to hear it read out from the Bible, in plain words that we cannot mistake; and then the next verse rests one so: 'Fear ye not, therefore: ye are of more value than many sparrows.'

   "Oh Lollie, it is good in a great, full, 'terrible' city like London, to remember that our Father numbers the very hairs of our head. It is good to belong to Him. That is the thought with which I want to go to sleep to-night, so I will leave you now.

"Good-by dear, until to-morrow."

HOW HE BECAME A SOLDIER.

ONE day I was walking through the streets of York, in England. I saw a little way ahead, a soldier coming toward me. He had the red uniform on of the infantry—the dress of the army. I knew at once when I saw him that he was a soldier.

When he came near me, I stopped him. I said, "My good man, if you have no objections, I would like to ask you a few questions."

"Certainly, sir," said he.

"Well, then, I would like to know how you first became a soldier?"

"Yes, sir, I will tell you. You see, sir, I wanted to become a soldier, and the recruiting officer was in our town, and I went up to him and told him I wanted to enlist.

"'Well, sir,' he said, 'all right.'

"And the first thing he did, sir, he took an English shilling out of his pocket, sir, and put it into my hand. The very moment, sir, a recruiting-sergeant puts a shilling into your hand, sir, you are a soldier."

I said to myself, "That is the very illustration I want."

That man was a free man at one time—he could go here and there, do just what he liked, but the moment the shilling was put into his hand, he was subject to the rules of war, and Queen Victoria could send him anywhere and make him obey the rules and regulations of the army. He is a soldier the very minute he takes the shilling. He has not got to wait to put on the uniform. And when you ask me how a man may be converted at once, I answer, just the same as that man became a soldier. The citizen becomes a soldier in a minute, and from being a free man becomes subject to the command of others. The moment you take Christ into your heart, that moment your name is written in the roll of heaven.

ST. BONIFACE FELLING THE OAK.

THE OLD OAK TREE.

DO you remember about the two gods, Woden and Thor that the Germans used to worship a great many years ago? Woden was supposed to be very wise, because two ravens kept whispering to him all the time, about what was going on here. The sun and moon were his eyes. What makes the moon paler than the sun? Now there is hardly a schoolboy who cannot give the true reason, but what do you think these Germans said, long ago? Why, that Woden gave the sight of one eye to pay for a very large drink out of the well of wisdom; and the name of that one eye was "moon" so of course it has been dull ever since. Thor, his son, was a very fierce and terrible god; all the oak trees were sacred to him. Once there came among these Germans, a missionary named St. Boniface. A great many of them listened to his story of the true God, and believed on Him. Now there was a very huge and beautiful oak tree, sacred to Thor; the heathen used to go under it to worship him, and even the Christians were afraid to touch it because it was sacred to Thor. St. Boniface talked with the people about it, asked them if they did not believe that Thor was able to take care of the tree if he was a god. Then he offered to cut down the tree. One day, all his ministers gathered with him about the tree, carrying crosses, and the woodman came with his axe, and the frightened people stood watching and trembling for fear of Thor's awful anger; and the tree was cut down, and Thor made no motion, nor in any way showed that he was anything but a wooden god. For this reason a large number of people lost their faith in him, and declared that they were going to worship the God of whom St. Boniface told them.

MARY BURTON IN LONDON. [Cont.]

   "MY DEAR LOLLIE,— I am just home from a visit to the Bethnal Green Museum. It is a lovely place in which to spend a morning. Do you know about it? James the First had the ground on which it is built given to the poor. It is said that all around the Museum at that time were bare fields, but now it is a crowded city. The building itself is ugly I think. It is all of dark red brick; the front is arched, but the arches are not graceful looking. I told Stacey Livermore that the building looked very much like the Union depot at Marysville. Inside it is just a great world's fair, all sorts of things on exhibition. There is a department for animal products, and one for vegetable products, and one for minerals, and one for metals, and one for wooden things. How much does that tell you about what I saw? I ought to pick out some one thing of special value and describe it; that is the way Mr. Burnham says we must write letters of interest from abroad; but do you believe I can do it? You see, the trouble is, I looked at so many things, they just whirl around in my brain, a mass of color and confusion, and I can't get anything out of them. One of these days I'll settle on something and describe it perhaps. The prettiest thing I saw, that had anything to do with the Museum, was the fountain just in front of the main entrance. It was perfectly lovely! Exquisite vases, and cups, and carved figures, and the water streamed in such graceful jets from them all. It is made of majolica ware. 'What is majolica ware?' I asked Stacey Livermore.

   "'S'pose I know!' he answered, as if he were so much astonished at being asked. Then I was determined to know about it; so I asked auntie, and Mrs. McMartin, and her niece, a young lady who knows everything—except about majolica ware; I couldn't get a bit of information as to that. So I waited for Mr. Burnham to come up, and tried him. Of course he knew. He said it depended on whether I meant what was it now, or what it was once when the Italians first began to use the word. I said I wanted to know from the beginning. So he told me. The Italians called a certain kind of earthen-ware by that name, because the first that they ever saw came from Majorca. After awhile the same kind of ware was made at Faenza, so people stopped saying 'majolica' and said 'faience' instead; a prettier name I think, don't you? In these days, he says the name majolica is used again, and people mean by it anything made out of colored clay, and coated with a white opaque varnish which makes it look like the original faience. I didn't like to ask him what 'opaque' meant, so I had to wait until I could get to a dictionary; then I was astonished to find that it only meant something that couldn't be seen through!

   "A beautifully carved figure of St. George and the dragon is on the top of the fountain. That was another thing about which I had to ask questions. I really wish I knew 'anything!' Still I didn't learn much. Stacey said St. George was a man who lived a great many years ago, and they made a saint of him. Now of course I knew that. As to the dragon, there was a story that he had rushed upon such a creature and killed it, and saved the life of a king's daughter by so doing; but who the king's daughter was, and how it came to happen, or whether there did really anything happen to make the legend out of, and if not, who first got it up, he didn't know. Stacey doesn't know much, now that's a fact; neither do I; but I do mean to study hard when I get home. I have been saying some of those things to Mr. Burnham to-night, and the answer he made was just exactly like him: 'But with all your getting, get wisdom.' That sounds as though the Bible thought there was one thing worth being called wisdom, doesn't it? I know Mr. Burnham thinks there is nothing so important as that kind of wisdom. Well, so do I, of course; but then comes the question, if I truly think so, why don't I get that? Aren't people queer, Lollie? I mustn't write any more. Auntie says my letters are always too long. Do you think so?

"Your loving Mary."

THREE GREAT MEN.

THEIR names were Solon, Cyrus, and Crœsus. Solon was one of seven very wise men, who lived in Greece between five and six hundred years before Christ was born. Among other things he did was to make a set of laws by which to govern the country.

image040
CRŒSUS BEFORE CYRUS.

Some of them were queer, and in these days we should not think them very wise. One was, that if a man was thought to be dangerous to the best interests of the country, the people could banish him for ten years; his name would be written on an oyster shell by any person who did not like him, then the shells were all thrown into a great ship, and by and by they were counted, and if they reached a certain number, the man was banished. Suppose there were such a rule in this country and these days, about boys! I wonder how many would be banished! At one time, Solon went to visit the famous king Crœsus, who lived in Lydia. He, you know, was very rich; he asked Solon (who was called a philosopher), who he thought was the happiest man in the world; and Solon answered, the one who did right, was neither rich, nor poor, had good children, and died bravely. Crœsus did not like this, and when he asked the wise man plainly what he thought of him, and received the answer, "Call no man happy until he is dead," he was more vexed still.

About that time, he was planning to go to war with Cyrus who was king of the Medes and Persians; you can read about him in the Bible. Crœsus decided to ask the oracles what he would better do, and to prove whether they knew what they were talking about, he said the oracle at Delphi must tell him what he was doing. This was the answer he received:

"Lo, on my sense striketh the smell of a shell-covered tortoise. Boiling on the fire, with the flesh of a lamb, in a cauldron. Brass is the vessel below brass is the cover above it."

Now it happened that Crœsus, at that time, was boiling a tortoise and a lamb together, in a brass dish! So then, he felt sure that the oracle knew everything, and asked it whether he should go to war; it replied, that if he did, a great kingdom would be overthrown. As this was just what he wanted to have happen to the kingdom of Cyrus, he concluded that that was what the oracle meant, and went to war. But it was his own kingdom that was taken; the city of Sardis was burned, and when he himself was about to be killed, he remembered what the wise man, Solon had said: "Call no man happy till he is dead," and feeling how wise a saying it was, he cried out, "Oh Solon! Solon!"

Then king Cyrus wanted to know what he meant by that, and he told him of Solon. This interested Cyrus very much, and he concluded to save Crœsus' life. O, the poor men, who were so wise, and yet so ignorant! They knew nothing about the Lord Jesus Christ, who has conquered even death, so that those who belong to him need not wait until they die to be called happy; but are just as sure of happiness as though the river of death were already passed.

CHEOPS.

"CHEOPS!" said Albert, turning the paper which had but that word written on it, upside down, and almost inside out in his effort to make it read something else. "Now I 'should' like to know what a fellow was going to do with that?"

"It means, chops," said his young sister, leaning over his shoulder and studying the paper carefully. "He has made a little quill that looks like an 'e,' but he didn't mean to, and it means chops, like what we had for breakfast, Albert."

image041
VIEW OF GALLERY IN THE GREAT PYRAMID.

"Oh!" said Albert. "What an idea!" Then he leaned his head back and shouted, with laughter. "Think of Professor Strongworth giving me mutton chops for a subject to write an essay about!"

"Well," said the little sister, positively, "he 'has,' anyhow."

Albert was only ten, and it must be confessed that when the box was passed with subjects for essays therein, he had drawn a hard one for a boy of his age. For the rest of the evening, he pored over books, talking now and then with father, or Aunt Carrie. His first discovery, he announced in an astonished tone, "I declare, it is a 'man!'"

The next morning his essay was ready; here is a copy of it:

"CHEOPS."

   "This is the name of a man who lived in Egypt about three thousand years before Christ came. He was the king. He had a good many names. Khufu, and Suphis, and Chemnis, and Chembres, and Cheops. I think the last three names mean the same thing. Some people say Cheops was a tyrant, others say he wasn't; but I have studied a good deal about him, and I think he was. He built a pyramid, at least his money built it, the largest pyramid in the world, and its name is Cheops. Some people say he had the temple closed and wouldn't let his subjects go there to say their prayers, because it would take time. I don't know how that is, but I know it took a hundred thousand men ten years to bring stone enough for the pyramid. This stone is very beautiful, hard like granite, and all sprinkled over with red and black, and when polished, shines like diamonds. Think of a hundred thousand men working ten years, to bring stone to make a grave to bury old Cheops in! It took twenty years to finish the pyramid, and nobody knows how much it cost. I suppose he wanted to build the finest pyramid that ever would be, and he did, and I wonder what good it does him now?"

image042
DISTANT VIEW OF THE PYRAMIDS.

   "The way they built pyramids, was this: first a little pyramid was built, with steps to go up it, and a little stone room, well finished. Then they built a kind of covering to this, and another, and another, and another, until they got it as large as they wanted it. The last covering was of very beautiful stone, like this red and black stone which Cheops used; only I guess none of the other pyramid builders used the same kind. Oh, yes, they did, too; for a man named Khafra who was either Cheop's son or his brother, it was so long ago that everybody seems to have forgotten which, built a house in the desert, all of this red and black granite, or stone of Assouan, except where here and there he put a little alabaster. Nobody knows why he built it, nor what he built it for, nor in fact whether he ever built it at all, only it is named for him. The work is very beautiful, but, oh dear! How many years the people have all been dead. What good did it all do? I wonder if they took care of their souls and went to live in 'the house that is not made with hands.' Isn't it strange to think that perhaps some day I shall see Cheops?"

TWO ROSES.

ON a straggling, wayside bush,
  Where the robins sing,
Out of sight of careless eyes,
  Two wild roses swing.
 
Both are fair as fair can be,
  Swinging to and fro,
Greeting, though unnoticed,
  All who past them go.
 
Nodding there, so sweetly,
  Almost out of reach;
Soon a ray of sunlight,
  Falls upon them each.
 
So, quietly and peacefully,
  Each has passed its life;
Which, in the end, with gladness,
  And sunshine bright, is rife.
 
May not these two roses, teach
  Lessons to us all.
Living patiently for others
  God's smile will on us fall.

A "TRULY" STORY.

"NOW, what I want," said little Neelie, creeping on to the old chest in the attic, and settling herself comfortably, while the warm summer rain pattered on the roof overhead,—"what I want is a 'truly' story. I'm just sick and tired of make-believe stories. I want to hear about some peoples who said things and did things, just as you and I and mamma and lots of folks do."

"Well," said sister Kate, remembering a wonderful story which she knew was true, "'I' like true stories, too, and I've got a perfectly splendid one to tell you.

"Once, a great many years ago, there was a good young man made a slave by some wicked people; they got him in a war, some way, and they made him take care of ever so many horses, and treated him very cruelly. He had a kind uncle who tried and tried to get the wicked king to let him come home; but he wouldn't,—he said that a piece of gold that would weigh ten pounds would have to be paid before the young man could be free. His poor uncle could not get so much money,—that is an 'awful' lot, Neelie,—so the man had to stay a slave.

"'Most everybody used to keep slaves then, and the young man's uncle had one whose name was Leo. One day he came to his master and told him if he would let him go where his nephew was, and stay a good while, he would get him free. So the uncle told him to go.

"So Leo went away to the country where the young man was. Every day he watched for a chance to speak to him; but the slaves were guarded so carefully that he could get no chance. He saw him go by with horses, and he saw that he was ragged and dirty, and looked very dreadful. At last Leo went to a man and said, 'I want you to sell me for a slave to that chief who keeps so many horses; you may have all the money that he will give for me; I want to be his slave.'"

"What did he do that for?" asked horrified Neelie.

"You listen," said the historian, "and you'll see. So Leo was sold for a slave to the same wicked chief who owned his young master. He was taken to the chief, who asked him what he could do, and he said he could cook beautifully. So he was tried, and when they found he was a wonderful cook, they gave him the cooking to do. His master liked him very much, and made him a kind of ruler over all the other slaves. So he saw the young man, who used to be very rich, every day; but he shook his head at him, and made signs that they must not pretend to know each other. He had a plan to make the young man free, but he knew he must wait, and wait, and be very patient; so he waited a whole long year.

"One day Leo made up his mind that the time had come. He went down where the poor, sad young man was sitting, watching his horses, and sat down with his back turned to him, so that nobody would think they were talking together. He said:

"'It is time to go home. When you put the horses in the stable to-night, don't go to sleep; be ready for the first call.'

"That day the chief had company, and one of the company—a man who liked to make fun—said to Leo,—

"'Look here! Tell the truth,—don't you intend to take one of your master's horses and run away, some night, to your own home?'

"What do you think Leo said? Why, he said,—

"'Oh, yes; I mean to do it this very night.'

"And he told the truth,—he 'did' mean to; but he laughed when he said it, and the man thought he was saying it for fun, and laughed too, and said,—

"'Well, see that you don't carry off anything of mine.'

"And that very night Leo and the young man escaped. They had a dreadful time. They had to swim a deep river in the night. And once some men who had been sent to catch them rode so close, on their horses, that they could hear them talk; and they said, if they caught those two slaves, one should be hung, and the other cut into little bits of pieces."

"Oh, my!" said Neelie, with a shudder.

"But they got safely home; and 'then' wasn't the uncle glad!"

"What did he give Leo?" asked the little audience.

"Oh, I was going to tell you. Leo, you see, was born a slave, and thought he would always have to be a slave; but the good uncle gave him his freedom. He took him to the church and opened every door in it, as a sign that he was free. Then he gave him land and a house, and treated him just like a friend. And that's all."

"Is it a truly story?" asked Neelie.

"Oh, yes; it is,—every word."

"Whereabouts is it in the Geography?"

"Oh, it was away off in Rome, where they kept slaves."

Neelie was still for a few minutes; then she said:

"It is a nice story, and Leo was good; but he wasn't so good as Jesus, was he, Kate? 'He' stayed ever and ever so many years out of heaven, and had a dreadful time, and was killed, wasn't he, Kate?"

"Oh, Neelie!" said Kate. "What a queer little thing you are!"

THE GUESSING GAME.

THE boys had been playing ball, and croquet, and tag, and I don't know how many other running games, all the afternoon. At last they sat down to rest, and play a guessing game which Charlie Wood said he originated. One of their number was selected to tell a true story, leaving out names and dates, and the boys were each to have two chances to guess it. Arthur Dunlap was the one chosen to give the story.

"Well," he said,—all their stories began with "Well,"—"there was once a man famous for being a—well, a tyrant, among other things, and a sharp, keen man. He had a place of power in the government, but people hated him because he was unjust."

image045

"He was a good deal of a scholar, and he thought he was a poet. Once he made a poem, and called on another scholar in the town to listen to it, and say what he thought of it. The man was honest enough to find some fault with it, and the old tyrant was so angry that he had him sent to prison. A good many weeks or months afterwards—I forget which—the poet composed another piece; he read it over carefully, and decided it was the best thing he had ever written. The more he thought about it, the more anxious he was to have the scholar whom he had sent to prison hear it; he knew he was a good judge of poetry. Finally, he sent for him to come and listen to the poem. When the old fellow had finished reading it, he looked around to the prisoner,—sure, this time, that he would be praised. But what did the man do but turn to the soldiers who were guarding him, and, shaking his head, say, 'Carry me back to prison.'

"The tyrant could understand a sharp thing when he heard it, and he was so amused with the man's wit and courage that he laughed and forgave him. Now guess his name and his country."

This was not an easy thing to do. The boys all looked puzzled.

"I haven't the least idea who it is," said Horace, who was always marked high in history. "I don't believe I ever heard of him."

"Oh, yes, you have; you are well acquainted. I heard you talking about him last week."

"What did I say?"

"Ah, that would be as good as telling!" said Arthur, shaking his head.

"When did it happen? This century?" asked one.

"No; nor the last, not the one before it, nor the one before that; it is 'very' ancient."

"B. C.?" asked young Willard.

"Yes, sir; B. C. almost four hundred years."

"What part of the world? North, south, east, or west?"

"Oh, I may as well tell you it was in Sicily, and the name of the city is one that Dick, here, is well acquainted with."

"Syracuse," said Dick, promptly.

But even then the boys couldn't guess.

"You'll have to hint what I was saying about him," said Horace.

To this all the boys agreed.

And so Arthur said it was something about a friend of his, and a sword.

Thereupon two of them shouted, "We know!"

And a third said, "Oh, Dionysius, of course; but I never heard that story of him before."
