How to UseThisBook
This book teaches you to build a small but fully working Large Language Model (LLM)
with your own hands, in plain Python and PyTorch. No magic libraries hide the important
parts: you will write the tokenizer, the transformer, the training loop and the text
generator yourself, and you will understand every line.
What you will build: a GPT-style model of roughly 1 to 85 million parameters (you choose
the size), trained on your own text (notes, books, code, articles, chat logs, company
documents) and then fine-tuned for a specific purpose.
What you need: basic Python (functions, classes, lists). Everything else, including
PyTorch, is explained as we go.
How each chapter works:
1. Idea: a plain-language explanation of what the part does and why.
2. How it works: the mechanics, with small examples.
3. Code: a complete file you can copy, run and modify.
4. Checkpoint: a quick test so you know it works before moving on.
By the end you will have these files, built one by one: clean.py , bpe.py , prepare.py ,
model.py , train.py , sample.py and sft.py .
Contents (Index)
Start here: Chapter 0, Foundations Before You Build, comes right before Chapter 1. It
explains the ideas you need before any code: neural networks, tensors, probability, loss,
gradient descent, PyTorch and compute. Read it first; it takes about 30 minutes.

0.2What an LLM is, and whatitis not
A large language model is a program that has learned, from a lot of text, how likely each
possible next piece of text is. Give it "The cat sat on the" and it scores every token it
knows; "mat" scores high, "carburetor" scores low. It then picks one token, adds it to the
text, and repeats.
What this means in practice:

Page 5 of 56
It is not a database or a search engine. It does not look facts up. Whatever it "knows"
is compressed into its parameters as statistical patterns.
It is not a rule engine. Nobody programmed grammar or logic into it. These abilities
appear because predicting text well requires them.
It optimizes for plausible, not for true. A fluent but false sentence can score highly.
This is called hallucination, and it is why you must test model output.
It only knows its training data. The model you build will write like your data and know
what your data contains, nothing more. This is the single most important fact for
planning a custom model.
"Large" is relative. Frontier models have hundreds of billions of parameters; the
models in this book have 1 to 90 million. Same idea, much smaller scale.
0.3 Machine learning in one page
Traditional programming means you write the rules. Machine learning means you show
examples and let the computer find the rules. Every ML system has three ingredients:
1. A model: a function with adjustable numbers (parameters).
2. A loss: a score for how wrong the model currently is.
3. An optimizer: a procedure that adjusts the parameters to lower the loss.
The basic building block is the neuron: multiply each input by a weight, add them up, add a
bias, and pass the result through a non-linear activation function (such as GELU).
output = activation( w1*x1 + w2*x2 + ... + bias )
A layer is many neurons side by side; a neural network is layers stacked. The activation
function matters: without it, stacking many layers would collapse into one simple linear
function and could not learn language. A network is therefore a very large formula with
millions of knobs, and training is the search for good knob settings.
0.4The only math you need
Three ideas cover almost everything in this book.
Vector: a list of numbers, such as the 384 numbers that represent one token.
Dot product: multiply two vectors element by element and add the results. A large
value means the vectors point the same way (they are "similar"). Attention is built on
this.
Build Your Own LLM From Scratch — A Step-by-Step Guide Book
Page 6 of 56
Matrix multiplication: applying a whole grid of weights to a vector (or to many vectors
at once). Every layer of the model is a matrix multiplication.
import torch
a = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]) # a vector, shape (3,)
M = torch.tensor([[1., 0.], [0., 1.], [1., 1.]]) # a matrix, shape (3,
2)
print(torch.dot(a, a)) # 1*1 + 2*2 + 3*3 = tensor(14.)
print(a @ M) # shape (3,) times (3, 2) gives shape (2,):
tensor([4., 5.])
The shape rule: when you multiply (n, k) @ (k, m) , the two inner numbers must match
and the result is (n, m) . When code crashes, nine times out of ten the shapes disagree.
Make it a habit to print(x.shape) while you build.
0.5 Probability and softmax
The model's final output for each position is a list of raw scores, one per token, called
logits. Logits can be any number, positive or negative. Softmax converts them into a
probability distribution: every value between 0 and 1, all adding up to exactly 1.
import torch
scores = torch.tensor([2.0, 1.0, 0.1])
probs = torch.softmax(scores, dim=0)
print(probs) # about [0.66, 0.24, 0.10]
print(probs.sum()) # 1.0
The biggest score gets the biggest share, but not all of it. To generate text we then sample
from these probabilities, so the likeliest token is chosen most often but not always. That
randomness is why the same prompt can produce different text, and it is what the
temperature setting in Chapter 9 controls.
0.6 Loss and cross-entropy
To train, we need one number that says how bad the predictions are. For next-token
prediction we use cross-entropy: look at the probability p the model gave to the token
that actually came next, and take the negative natural logarithm.
Build Your Own LLM From Scratch — A Step-by-Step Guide Book
Page 7 of 56
\text{loss} = -\ln p_{\text{correct}}
That last row is the number you will check in Chapter 7. Training is the process of pushing
this average loss down.
0.7 How learning works: gradient descent and backpropagation
Imagine the loss as the height of a landscape, where every parameter is a direction you
can walk in. You are standing somewhere on a foggy hillside and want to reach the valley.
The gradient tells you which way is steepest uphill for every parameter at once; you step
the opposite way. The size of each step is the learning rate: too small and you crawl, too
large and you overshoot and bounce around.
Backpropagation is the efficient algorithm that computes the gradient for all millions of
parameters in one backward sweep through the network. You never write it yourself:
PyTorch's autograd records every operation during the forward pass and replays it
backwards when you call loss.backward() .
Here is the whole idea at toy scale: a model with just two parameters learns the rule y =
2x + 1 from examples.
Probability given to the correct
token
Loss Meaning
0.90 0.11 Confident and right
0.50 0.69 Unsure
0.10 2.30 Mostly wrong
0.01 4.61 Very wrong
1 in 2,000 (pure guessing) 7.60 The starting loss of an untrained model with a
2,000-token vocabulary

Page 8 of 56
import torch
x = torch.linspace(-1, 1, 20).unsqueeze(1) # 20 example inputs
y = 2 * x + 1 # the answers we want it to
discover
model = torch.nn.Linear(1, 1) # two parameters: a weight and
a bias
opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1)
for step in range(200):
loss = ((model(x) - y) ** 2).mean() # how wrong are we?
opt.zero_grad() # forget old gradients
loss.backward() # compute new gradients
opt.step() # take a small step downhill
print(model.weight.item(), model.bias.item()) # close to 2.0 and 1.0
This is exactly the loop of Chapter 8. A GPT differs only in that the model has millions of
parameters instead of two, and the loss is cross-entropy instead of squared error.

Autograd in three lines:
import torch
x = torch.tensor(3.0, requires_grad=True)
y = x ** 2
y.backward()
print(x.grad) # tensor(6.), because the slope of x squared is 2x
0.9 Language as numbers:tokens, embeddings, context
A computer cannot read letters, so text goes through three conversions that you will build
in Chapters 4 and 6:
1. Tokens: text is cut into pieces (words, word parts or characters) and each piece gets
an integer ID from a fixed list called the vocabulary.
2. Embeddings: each ID is swapped for a learned vector of numbers. During training,
tokens used in similar ways end up with similar vectors, so meaning becomes
geometry.
3. Context window: the model can only read a fixed number of tokens at once
( block_size ). Anything older is invisible to it. This is its entire working memory.
Word order matters, so the model also adds a position signal. Then attention lets each
token look back at earlier ones and pull in what is relevant, for example connecting "it" to
the noun it refers to. That mechanism is the heart of the transformer, and Chapter 6 builds
it step by step.
You will see What it does
model.train() and model.eval() Switch dropout on (training) or off (generation,
evaluation)
torch.no_grad() Skip gradient bookkeeping when you do not
need it, which saves memory
.to(device) Move a model or tensor to the GPU or CPU

0.10 Pretraining,fine-tuning and inference
A model straight after pretraining is a base model: it continues text but does not follow
instructions. A chat or instruct model is a base model that was fine-tuned on question
and answer examples. You train once and then use the model many times, so training cost
is paid up front.
0.11 Practicalfoundations: overfitting, splits and hardware
Generalization and overfitting. The goal is a model that works on text it has never seen. A
model that memorizes its training text scores well there and badly on new text. That is
why we always hold back validation data that the model never trains on (Chapter 5) and
compare the two losses (Chapter 8). The smaller your dataset, the sooner overfitting
appears.
Memory. Each parameter is a number that must be stored. Training with the AdamW
optimizer in 32-bit precision needs about 16 bytes per parameter: 4 for the weight, 4 for
its gradient, and 8 for the optimizer's two running averages. Activations add more on top.
Running a trained model needs only 2 to 4 bytes per parameter.

This table is why this book stays small, and why for big models the practical route is LoRA
fine-tuning, not training from scratch.
CPU versus GPU. Training is mostly matrix multiplication, thousands of independent
multiply-adds. A GPU does them in parallel, so it is typically many times faster than a CPU.
Small models still work on a CPU, just slowly.
Good habits from day one. Fix random seeds when comparing runs, change one setting at
a time, and write down the validation loss of every run.
0.12Building responsibly
Data rights: use text you own or are licensed to use. Public does not always mean free
to train on.
Privacy: models memorize. Remove personal details, passwords and keys before
training, and never train on other people's private messages.
Bias: a model repeats the patterns, including the unfair ones, in its data. Read samples
of your data before you train.
Trust: never present model output as verified fact. State clearly when text was
machine-generated.
Honest limits: a small model trained on little data is a learning tool and a style imitator,
not an authority.

1.TheBig Picture:What an LLM Really Is
The one idea behind everything
An LLM does exactly one job: given some text, predict the next piece of text. That is all.
If you type "The capital of France is", the model assigns a high probability to " Paris". To
write a whole paragraph, it predicts one token, adds it to the text, and predicts again.
Chatting, summarizing, coding and translating are all this same trick, repeated.
Training is how the model learns these probabilities. We show it huge amounts of text, ask
"what comes next?" at every position, compare its guess with the real answer, and nudge
its internal numbers (the parameters or weights) so the next guess is slightly better.
Repeat millions of times.
Question Short answer
What single task is an LLM trained to do? Predict the next token given the tokens
before it
What are parameters? The adjustable numbers inside the model
that training changes
Why does an untrained model with a 2,000-
token vocabulary start at a loss near 7.6?
It guesses uniformly, and the natural log of
2,000 is about 7.6
What does the learning rate control? How big each parameter update is

trains on?

Frontier models have hundreds of billions of parameters and cost millions of dollars to

at every size, so a small model teaches you exactly how the big ones work.

Honest expectation: a model trained from scratch on a few megabytes of text will imitate

3. Preparing Your Own Data
Why data matters most
A language model is a compressed copy of its training text. It can only reproduce the
style, vocabulary and facts it has seen. Clean, relevant data beats a large pile of messy
data, especially for small models.
Where to get data
Source Good for
Your own notes, emails, blog posts,
journals
A personal writing-style model
Build Your Own LLM From Scratch — A Step-by-Step Guide Book
Page 16 of 56
Privacy warning: the model memorizes what it reads. Never train on passwords, API keys,
private messages of other people, or anything you would not want it to repeat.
How much data do you need?
A useful guideline from research (the "Chinchilla" rule) is about 20 training tokens per
parameter. For an 11M-parameter model that is about 220 million tokens, close to 1 GB of
text. You will often have far less, and that is fine, with these adjustments:
Under 1 MB of text: use the Tiny config, or the model will memorize everything.
1 to 20 MB: use Tiny or Small, keep dropout on, and stop when validation loss stops
improving (Chapter 8 shows how).
20 MB and up: Small or Medium works well.
Rough conversion: 1 MB of English text is about 300,000 tokens with the tokenizer in this
book.
Clean and combine your files
Put all your .txt files into raw/ . This script normalizes whitespace and merges
everything into one training file.

TinyStories dataset Very clean simple English, ideal for tiny
models
Company manuals, FAQs, support tickets A domain or customer-support model
Wikipedia article dumps Factual, encyclopedic text

# clean.py
import pathlib
import re
def clean(text):
text = text.replace("\r\n", "\n") # unify line endings
text = re.sub(r"[ \t]+", " ", text) # collapse spaces and tabs
text = re.sub(r"\n{3,}", "\n\n", text) # at most one blank line
return text.strip()
files = sorted(pathlib.Path("raw").glob("**/*.txt"))
parts = [clean(f.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="ignore")) for f in
files]
pathlib.Path("data").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
pathlib.Path("data/input.txt").write_text("\n\n".join(parts), encoding="utf8")

4.Tokenization:TurningTextinto Numbers
The idea
Neural networks only understand numbers. A tokenizer converts text to a list of integers
(token IDs) and back. The choice of how to split text matters:
Method Example for
"unhappiness"
Pros and cons
Characterlevel
u, n, h, a, p, p, i, n, e, s, s Tiny vocabulary, but sequences get very long
Word-level unhappiness Short sequences, but unknown words break it
and vocabulary is huge

Page 18 of 56
How Byte PairEncoding (BPE) works
BPE starts with single bytes and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into
a new token.
Take the string aaabdaaabac :
1. Most frequent pair is aa . Replace it with a new symbol Z . Text becomes ZabdZabac .
2. Most frequent pair is now ab . Replace it with Y . Text becomes ZYdZYac .
3. Most frequent pair is ZY . Replace it with X . Text becomes XdXac .
The list of merges (in order) is the tokenizer. To encode new text, replay the same merges
in the same order. Because we start from raw bytes, any text in any language can be
encoded, so there are never "unknown" tokens.
Quick-start alternative: character-level
For a first experiment on a tiny file, a character tokenizer is just five lines:
text = open("data/input.txt", encoding="utf-8").read()
chars = sorted(set(text))
stoi = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(chars)} # char -> id
itos = {i: c for c, i in stoi.items()} # id -> char
encode = lambda s: [stoi[c] for c in s]
decode = lambda ids: "".join(itos[i] for i in ids)
The rest of this book uses BPE, because it makes the model see more text per training
step.
Code: aBPEtokenizer from scratch
# bpe.py
import re
from collections import Counter
# Splits text into word-like pieces so merges never cross word boundaries
Method Example for
"unhappiness"
Pros and cons
Subword
(BPE)
un, happiness Best balance; used by GPT models

Page 19 of 56
PAT = re.compile(r"\s?\w+|\s?[^\w\s]+|\s+")
class BPETokenizer:
def __init__(self):
self.merges = {} # (id_a, id_b) ->
new id
self.vocab = {i: bytes([i]) for i in range(256)} # id -> bytes
self.cache = {}
@staticmethod
def _merge(ids, pair, new_id):
out, i = [], 0
while i < len(ids):
if i < len(ids) - 1 and ids[i] == pair[0] and ids[i + 1] ==
pair[1]:
out.append(new_id)
i += 2
else:
out.append(ids[i])
i += 1
return out
def train(self, text, vocab_size):
words = Counter(PAT.findall(text)) # piece ->
count
seqs = {w: list(w.encode("utf-8")) for w in words} # piece ->
byte ids
for new_id in range(256, vocab_size):
stats = Counter()
for w, count in words.items():
s = seqs[w]
for pair in zip(s, s[1:]):
stats[pair] += count
if not stats:
break
best = max(stats, key=stats.get) # most
frequent pair
for w in seqs:
seqs[w] = self._merge(seqs[w], best, new_id)
self.merges[best] = new_id
self.vocab[new_id] = self.vocab[best[0]] + self.vocab[best[1]]
if new_id % 200 == 0:
print(f"merge {new_id - 255}/{vocab_size - 256}")
Build Your Own LLM From Scratch — A Step-by-Step Guide Book
Page 20 of 56
def _encode_piece(self, piece):
if piece in self.cache:
return self.cache[piece]
ids = list(piece.encode("utf-8"))
while len(ids) >= 2:
pairs = set(zip(ids, ids[1:]))
pair = min(pairs, key=lambda p: self.merges.get(p, float("inf")))
if pair not in self.merges:
break
ids = self._merge(ids, pair, self.merges[pair])
self.cache[piece] = ids
return ids
def encode(self, text):
out = []
for piece in PAT.findall(text):
out.extend(self._encode_piece(piece))
return out
def decode(self, ids):
return b"".join(self.vocab[i] for i in ids).decode("utf-8",
errors="replace")
Testit

print(tok.decode(ids)) # must print exactly: Hello world!
Choosing the vocabulary size
Smaller (500 to 2,000): fits small datasets, longer sequences, trains faster to a decent
result. Recommended here.
Larger (30,000 to 100,000): what big models use; needs far more data, otherwise many
tokens are rarely seen.
Checkpoint: decode(encode(text)) returns exactly the original text.

5.Building theTraining Dataset
Next-token prediction: inputs and targets
Suppose your text became the tokens [5, 9, 2, 7] . We build two sequences, the
second shifted by one position:
At position 1 the model sees only 5 and must predict 9 . At position 2 it sees 5, 9 and
must predict 2 . One sequence of length T therefore gives T training examples at once.
The length T is called the context length or block_size : how far back the model can look.
Train and validation split
We keep 90% of the tokens for training and hide 10% as validation. The model never
learns from validation data, so its loss there tells us honestly whether the model is
learning real patterns or just memorizing.
Code: encode everything once
Encoding the full text once and saving it as a binary file makes training fast.
Position 1 2 3
Input x 5 9 2
Target y 9 2 7

6.Inside theTransformer:Embeddings and Attention
This is the heart of the book. A transformer is built from only a few simple parts, repeated
many times. We will meet each part, see what it does with a tiny example, and only then
assemble the full model in Chapter 7.
Build Your Own LLM From Scratch — A Step-by-Step Guide Book
Page 23 of 56
6.1 Notation:the shape ofthe data
Every tensor inside the model has three dimensions. Learn these letters now; they appear
in every code comment.
So a batch of text, after embedding, is a tensor of shape (B, T, C) .
6.2Embeddings: giving tokens meaning
A token ID such as 1042 is just a label. The model needs a rich vector of numbers it can
compute with. An embedding table is a matrix with one row per token ( vocab_size rows,
n_embd columns). Looking up token 1042 means reading row 1042. Those rows start
random and are learned during training, so tokens used in similar ways end up with similar
vectors.
Attention has no built-in sense of word order, so we also learn a position embedding: one
vector per position (0, 1, 2, up to block_size - 1 ). The input to the transformer is simply
the two added together:
x = token_embedding[token_id] + position_embedding[position]
6.3 Self-attention:tokens looking at each other
To predict the next word in "The cat sat on the ___", the model must connect "the" with
"cat" and "sat". Self-attention is the mechanism that lets every token look at the earlier
tokens and collect useful information from them.
Each token creates three vectors by multiplying its embedding with three learned
matrices:
Query (Q): "what am I looking for?"
Letter Meaning Example
B Batch size: how many sequences we process at
once
32
T Time: number of tokens in each sequence (the
context length)
256
C Channels: the size of the vector that represents
one token ( n_embd )
384
Build Your Own LLM From Scratch — A Step-by-Step Guide Book
Page 24 of 56
Key (K): "what do I contain?"
Value (V): "what information will I hand over if you pick me?"
The steps:
1. Compare the Query of the current token with the Key of every earlier token (a dot
product). A high score means "relevant".
2. Divide by the square root of the head size. This keeps scores small so the next step
stays stable.
3. Apply softmax, which turns the scores into weights that are positive and add up to 1.
4. Output the weighted average of the Values.
As one formula:
\mathrm{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \mathrm{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}
{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V
The causal mask. When training, the model sees the whole sentence at once, but it must
not peek at future tokens or it could simply copy the answer. We hide the future by
setting the scores of all later positions to minus infinity before the softmax, so their
weights become exactly 0. This is called causal (or masked) attention, and it is what
makes the model a text generator.
Here it is in 10 lines. Run it and watch the weights: row t only has non-zero values up to
column t .
Build Your Own LLM From Scratch — A Step-by-Step Guide Book
Page 25 of 56
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
B, T, C, head = 1, 4, 8, 8
x = torch.randn(B, T, C)
Wq, Wk, Wv = (torch.nn.Linear(C, head, bias=False) for _ in range(3))
q, k, v = Wq(x), Wk(x), Wv(x)
scores = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / head ** 0.5 # (B, T, T) how much
each token likes each other token
mask = torch.tril(torch.ones(T, T)) # lower-triangular
matrix of ones
scores = scores.masked_fill(mask == 0, float("-inf")) # hide the future
weights = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1) # every row sums to 1
out = weights @ v # (B, T, head) weighted
mix of values
print(weights[0])
The filled lower-left triangle is what each token may read; the empty upper-right triangle
is the future, which the mask hides. This is exactly the pattern your weights matrix
prints.
causal attention mask · 5 tokens
Build Your Own LLM From Scratch — A Step-by-Step Guide Book
Page 26 of 56
6.4 Multi-head attention: several views at once
One attention pattern is not enough. One head may track grammar, another may track
names, another may look at the previous token. Multi-head attention splits the C
channels into n_head groups and runs attention in each group in parallel. With C = 384
and n_head = 6 , each head works with 64 channels. The head outputs are concatenated
back to size C and mixed by one more linear layer (the projection).
6.5 Feed-forward network (MLP):thinking per token
Attention moves information between tokens. The feed-forward network then processes
each token on its own: expand the vector 4 times wider, apply a non-linearity (GELU), and
shrink back. This is where much of the model's stored knowledge lives, and it holds about
two thirds of the parameters.
6.6 Residual connections and LayerNorm: keeping deep networks trainable
Residual connection: each sub-layer adds its result to its own input, x = x +
sublayer(x) . The original signal always has a clear path through the network, which
makes gradients flow and deep stacks trainable.
LayerNorm: rescales each token vector to a stable mean and spread. We apply it
before each sub-layer (called "pre-norm"), the layout GPT-2 and most modern models
use.
Dropout: randomly zeroes a few values during training so the model cannot rely on any
single path. Essential for small datasets.
Checkpoint: run the 10-line attention example. The printed 4 by 4 matrix must be lowertriangular (zeros above the diagonal) with each row adding up to 1.
7. Assembling the Full GPT Model
7.1The recipe
One transformer block = LayerNorm, attention, residual add, LayerNorm, MLP, residual
add. The full GPT is:
1. Token embedding + position embedding
2. A stack of n_layer transformer blocks
3. A final LayerNorm
Build Your Own LLM From Scratch — A Step-by-Step Guide Book
Page 27 of 56
4. A linear language-model head that turns each token vector into vocab_size scores
(called logits), one per possible next token
Two small tricks are used: weight tying (the output head reuses the token-embedding
matrix, saving parameters and improving quality) and a small-variance weight
initialization (standard deviation 0.02) for stable early training.
Data flows top to bottom. The highlighted block is stacked n_layer times, and its shape
never changes, which is why you can make the model deeper just by raising n_layer .
GPT architecture · 6 steps, one repeated block

7.2 Code: model.py
# model.py
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.nn import functional as F
from dataclasses import dataclass
@dataclass
class GPTConfig:
vocab_size: int = 2000
block_size: int = 256 # context length T
n_layer: int = 6
n_head: int = 6
n_embd: int = 384 # channels C
dropout: float = 0.1
class CausalSelfAttention(nn.Module):
def __init__(self, cfg):
super().__init__()
assert cfg.n_embd % cfg.n_head == 0
self.n_head = cfg.n_head
self.dropout = cfg.dropout
self.qkv = nn.Linear(cfg.n_embd, 3 * cfg.n_embd, bias=False) # Q,
K, V in one matrix
self.proj = nn.Linear(cfg.n_embd, cfg.n_embd, bias=False)
self.resid_drop = nn.Dropout(cfg.dropout)
def forward(self, x):
B, T, C = x.shape
q, k, v = self.qkv(x).split(C, dim=2)
# (B, T, C) -> (B, n_head, T, head_size)
q = q.view(B, T, self.n_head, C // self.n_head).transpose(1, 2)
k = k.view(B, T, self.n_head, C // self.n_head).transpose(1, 2)
v = v.view(B, T, self.n_head, C // self.n_head).transpose(1, 2)
# fused, fast version of: softmax(q k^T / sqrt(d)) with causal mask,
times v
y = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(
q, k, v, is_causal=True,
dropout_p=self.dropout if self.training else 0.0)
y = y.transpose(1, 2).contiguous().view(B, T, C) # rejoin the heads
return self.resid_drop(self.proj(y))
Build Your Own LLM From Scratch — A Step-by-Step Guide Book
Page 29 of 56
class MLP(nn.Module):
def __init__(self, cfg):
super().__init__()
self.fc = nn.Linear(cfg.n_embd, 4 * cfg.n_embd)
self.proj = nn.Linear(4 * cfg.n_embd, cfg.n_embd)
self.drop = nn.Dropout(cfg.dropout)
def forward(self, x):
return self.drop(self.proj(F.gelu(self.fc(x))))
class Block(nn.Module):
def __init__(self, cfg):
super().__init__()
self.ln1 = nn.LayerNorm(cfg.n_embd)
self.attn = CausalSelfAttention(cfg)
self.ln2 = nn.LayerNorm(cfg.n_embd)
self.mlp = MLP(cfg)
def forward(self, x):
x = x + self.attn(self.ln1(x)) # residual around attention
x = x + self.mlp(self.ln2(x)) # residual around MLP
return x
class GPT(nn.Module):
def __init__(self, cfg):
super().__init__()
self.cfg = cfg
self.tok_emb = nn.Embedding(cfg.vocab_size, cfg.n_embd)
self.pos_emb = nn.Embedding(cfg.block_size, cfg.n_embd)
self.drop = nn.Dropout(cfg.dropout)
self.blocks = nn.ModuleList([Block(cfg) for _ in range(cfg.n_layer)])
self.ln_f = nn.LayerNorm(cfg.n_embd)
self.head = nn.Linear(cfg.n_embd, cfg.vocab_size, bias=False)
self.head.weight = self.tok_emb.weight # weight tying
self.apply(self._init)
def _init(self, m):
if isinstance(m, nn.Linear):
nn.init.normal_(m.weight, mean=0.0, std=0.02)
if m.bias is not None:
nn.init.zeros_(m.bias)
elif isinstance(m, nn.Embedding):
Build Your Own LLM From Scratch — A Step-by-Step Guide Book
Page 30 of 56
nn.init.normal_(m.weight, mean=0.0, std=0.02)
def forward(self, idx, targets=None):
B, T = idx.shape
assert T <= self.cfg.block_size, "sequence longer than block_size"
pos = torch.arange(T, device=idx.device)
x = self.drop(self.tok_emb(idx) + self.pos_emb(pos)) # (B, T, C)
for block in self.blocks:
x = block(x)
logits = self.head(self.ln_f(x)) # (B, T,
vocab_size)
loss = None
if targets is not None:
loss = F.cross_entropy(
logits.view(-1, logits.size(-1)), targets.view(-1),
ignore_index=-100) # -100 = "do
not train on this"
return logits, loss
@torch.no_grad()
def generate(self, idx, max_new_tokens, temperature=0.8, top_k=50):
for _ in range(max_new_tokens):
idx_cond = idx[:, -self.cfg.block_size:] # crop to the
context window
logits, _ = self(idx_cond)
logits = logits[:, -1, :] / max(temperature, 1e-5) # only the
last position matters
if top_k:
v, _ = torch.topk(logits, min(top_k, logits.size(-1)))
logits[logits < v[:, [-1]]] = float("-inf")
probs = F.softmax(logits, dim=-1)
next_id = torch.multinomial(probs, num_samples=1)
idx = torch.cat([idx, next_id], dim=1)
return idx

untrained model guesses uniformly among 2,000 tokens, and the natural log of 2,000 is
about 7.6. If your first loss is far from ln(vocab_size) , something is wrong.

8.Training the Model
8.1Whattraining actually does
Training repeats one cycle, thousands of times:
1. Sample a batch: pick random chunks of your text, giving inputs x and targets y
(Chapter 5).
Config n_layer n_head n_embd block_size Parameters (vocab
2,000)
Best for
Tiny 4 4 128 128 about 1.1M CPU, under 1 MB of data
Small 6 6 384 256 about 11.5M Free GPU, 1 to 20 MB of data
Medium 8 8 512 256 about 26M Free GPU, 20 MB and up
Large 12 12 768 512 about 87M 8 to 12 GB GPU, 100 MB and
up
Build Your Own LLM From Scratch — A Step-by-Step Guide Book
Page 32 of 56
2. Forward pass: the model predicts a probability for every possible next token at every
position.
3. Loss: cross-entropy measures how much probability the model gave to the correct
next token. Giving it 90% costs little; giving it 0.1% costs a lot.
4. Backward pass: autograd computes, for every parameter, how a tiny change would
change the loss (the gradient).
5. Update: the optimizer (AdamW) moves every parameter a small step in the direction
that lowers the loss. The step size is the learning rate.
The loss (highlighted) is the number you watch while training; the other four steps exist to
make it smaller.
8.2The knobs that matter
training loop · 5 steps, repeated
Setting Meaning Good starting value
learning_rate Size of each update step 6e-4 for small models
batch_size Sequences per step; bigger is
smoother
32 (lower if you run out of
memory)
block_size Context length T 256
max_iters Total training steps 3,000 to 10,000
dropout Fraction of values randomly zeroed 0.1 (use 0.2 for very small data)
weight_decay Gentle pull of weights toward zero 0.1
Build Your Own LLM From Scratch — A Step-by-Step Guide Book
Page 33 of 56
Learning-rate schedule. We start with a short warmup (the rate rises from near zero for
200 steps, because early gradients are noisy), then use cosine decay down to 10% of the
peak. Big steps early, fine steps late.

def get_lr(it):
if it < warmup_iters:
return learning_rate * (it + 1) / warmup_iters # linear
warmup
ratio = (it - warmup_iters) / max(1, max_iters - warmup_iters)
return min_lr + 0.5 * (1 + math.cos(math.pi * ratio)) * (learning_rate -
min_lr) # cosine decay
@torch.no_grad()
def estimate_loss():
model.eval()
out = {}
for split in ("train", "val"):
losses = torch.zeros(eval_iters)
for k in range(eval_iters):
x, y = get_batch(split)
with amp:
_, loss = model(x, y)
losses[k] = loss.item()
out[split] = losses.mean().item()
model.train()
return out
# ---------- training loop ----------
os.makedirs("out", exist_ok=True)
best_val, t0 = float("inf"), time.time()
for it in range(max_iters):
for g in opt.param_groups:
g["lr"] = get_lr(it)
if it % eval_interval == 0 or it == max_iters - 1:
L = estimate_loss()
print(f"step {it:5d} | train {L['train']:.3f} | val {L['val']:.3f} |
{time.time() - t0:.0f}s")
if L["val"] < best_val: # keep only
the best model

8.4 Reading the loss curve
The printed train and val numbers tell you everything.
Perplexity is simply exp(loss) : roughly how many tokens the model is "confused
between" at each step. A loss of 7.6 means confusion between about 2,000 tokens; a loss
of 3.0 means about 20. Lower is better, and what is achievable depends heavily on your
data.
Checkpoint: out/ckpt.pt exists and the validation loss fell well below 7.6.

Page 37 of 56
1. Encode your prompt into token IDs.
2. Run the model and look only at the scores for the last position. These are the logits for
the next token.
3. Convert logits to probabilities with softmax and sample one token.
4. Append it to the sequence and go back to step 2.
The model never "plans" a sentence. It writes one token at a time, always reading
everything before it, and that is enough to produce coherent text.
9.2 Controlling creativity:temperature and top-k
For factual or domain text use low temperature (0.5 to 0.7). For stories and ideas use 0.9 to
1.0.

10.3 Preparing SFTdata
Create a file data/sft.jsonl with one JSON object per line:
{"prompt": "What are your opening hours?", "response": "We are open Monday to
Saturday, 9 AM to 6 PM."}
{"prompt": "How do I reset my password?", "response": "Open Settings, choose
Security, then tap Reset Password."}
Every example is turned into one piece of text with fixed markers:
### User:
What are your opening hours?
### Assistant:
We are open Monday to Saturday, 9 AM to 6 PM.<|end|>
The <|end|> marker teaches the model when to stop talking. Quality beats quantity: 300
clean, consistent examples are better than 3,000 sloppy ones. Keep each example shorter
than your block_size .
Loss masking. We only want the model to learn the answer, not to memorize the
questions. So we set the targets of the prompt part to -100 , which our model's loss
function ignores (you already saw ignore_index=-100 in model.py ).

10.4 LoRA:fine-tuning with a tiny number of new parameters
Full fine-tuning updates every weight. LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) freezes the original
weight matrix W and learns a small correction as the product of two thin matrices, B and
A :
W' = W + \frac{\alpha}{r} \, B A \qquad B \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{out} \times
r},\; A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d_{in}}
For a 384 by 384 layer, the full matrix has 147,456 values; a rank r = 8 correction has only
6,144 (about 4%). Benefits: far less memory, fast training, and you can keep many small
adapters (one per task) for the same base model. The same trick scales to billionparameter models.
The input flows through the frozen original weights and, in parallel, through the small
trainable pair. Their outputs are added, so training changes behavior without touching W .
10.5 Code: sft.py (fullfine-tuning or LoRA)
Run python sft.py data/sft.jsonl for full fine-tuning, or python sft.py
data/sft.jsonl lora for LoRA.
# sft.py
import json
import pickle
import random
import sys
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

from model import GPT, GPTConfig
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "mps" if
torch.backends.mps.is_available() else "cpu"
use_lora = "lora" in sys.argv
tok = pickle.load(open("data/tok.pkl", "rb"))
# ---------- LoRA ----------
class LoRALinear(nn.Module):
def __init__(self, base, r=8, alpha=16):
super().__init__()
self.base = base
for p in self.base.parameters():
p.requires_grad = False #
freeze original weights
self.A = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(r, base.in_features) * 0.01)
self.B = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(base.out_features, r)) # zeros:
starts as the original model
self.scale = alpha / r
def forward(self, x):
return self.base(x) + (x @ self.A.T @ self.B.T) * self.scale
def add_lora(model, r=8):
for p in model.parameters():
p.requires_grad = False
for blk in model.blocks:
blk.attn.qkv = LoRALinear(blk.attn.qkv, r)
blk.attn.proj = LoRALinear(blk.attn.proj, r)
def merge_lora(model): # fold
adapters back into W
for blk in model.blocks:
for name in ("qkv", "proj"):
layer = getattr(blk.attn, name)
if isinstance(layer, LoRALinear):
layer.base.weight.data += (layer.B @ layer.A) * layer.scale
setattr(blk.attn, name, layer.base)
# ---------- load the pretrained model ----------
ckpt = torch.load("out/ckpt.pt", map_location="cpu")
cfg = GPTConfig(**ckpt["cfg"])
model = GPT(cfg)

# ---------- build training examples ----------
def build(prompt, response):
p_ids = tok.encode(f"### User:\n{prompt}\n### Assistant:\n")
r_ids = tok.encode(response + "<|end|>")
ids = (p_ids + r_ids)[: cfg.block_size + 1]
labels = ([-100] * len(p_ids) + r_ids)[: cfg.block_size + 1] # no
loss on the prompt
return ids, labels
rows = [json.loads(line) for line in open(sys.argv[1], encoding="utf-8") if
line.strip()]
examples = [build(r["prompt"], r["response"]) for r in rows]
print(len(examples), "examples")
def make_batch(exs, bs):
batch = random.sample(exs, min(bs, len(exs)))
L = max(len(ids) for ids, _ in batch) - 1
x = torch.zeros(len(batch), L, dtype=torch.long)
y = torch.full((len(batch), L), -100, dtype=torch.long)
for k, (ids, labels) in enumerate(batch):
n = len(ids) - 1
x[k, :n] = torch.tensor(ids[:-1])
y[k, :n] = torch.tensor(labels[1:])
return x.to(device), y.to(device)
# ---------- train ----------
steps, bs = 300, 8
lr = 1e-3 if use_lora else 1e-4
params = [p for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad]
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(params, lr=lr, weight_decay=0.0)
model.train()
for step in range(steps):
x, y = make_batch(examples, bs)
_, loss = model(x, y)
opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
loss.backward()
torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(params, 1.0)
opt.step()

10.6Tips for good fine-tuning
Watch for overfitting: if the model repeats training answers word for word on new
questions, lower steps or add more varied examples.
Be consistent: the same style, the same format, no contradicting answers.
Include variety: ask the same thing in several different ways.
Test on questions you did not train on, and keep a small list of test prompts to
compare before and after.
Do not train on private data you would not want repeated, because the model can
reproduce it.

This small script lets you talk to your fine-tuned model in a loop. It wraps every question in
the same ### User: and ### Assistant: markers used during fine-tuning, and cuts the
answer at <|end|> .

11.Evaluating andTroubleshooting
11.1 How to know if your model is good
Numbers and your own eyes both matter.
1. Validation loss and perplexity. The lower the validation loss, the better the model
predicts text it has never seen. Compare runs only on the same validation data.
Build Your Own LLM From Scratch — A Step-by-Step Guide Book
Page 45 of 56
2. A fixed set of test prompts. Write 10 to 20 prompts that represent your real purpose.
After every training run, generate answers and compare them side by side. Human
judgement on your task is the real test.
3. A memorization check. If the model copies long stretches of your training text, it is
memorizing rather than learning. Paste a generated passage into this snippet:
train_text = open("data/input.txt", encoding="utf-8").read()
generated = "paste the model output here"
for i in range(0, len(generated) - 50, 50):
chunk = generated[i:i + 50]
if chunk in train_text:
print("verbatim copy:", repr(chunk))
Many verbatim copies mean overfitting: add data, raise dropout, or use a smaller preset.

12. Scaling Up and Modern Upgrades
12.1What really improves a model
Research on scaling laws gives a simple order of priorities for a fixed budget:
1. More and better data (the biggest lever for small models).
2. More training steps until validation loss stops improving.
3. A bigger model, but only if you have the data to feed it (about 20 tokens per
parameter).
4. Architecture tweaks, which give smaller but real gains.
12.2Training tricks for limited hardware
Gradient accumulation simulates a large batch on a small GPU: run several small batches,
add up the gradients, then take one optimizer step. Replace the training step in train.py
with:

A first upgrade to try, RMSNorm, is only a few lines. Replace each
nn.LayerNorm(cfg.n_embd) in model.py with it:
class RMSNorm(nn.Module):
def __init__(self, dim, eps=1e-6):
super().__init__()
self.eps = eps
self.weight = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(dim))
def forward(self, x):
return x * torch.rsqrt(x.pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True) + self.eps) *
self.weight
12.4 From your modelto a real assistant
The professional workflow most people use after learning the internals:
1. Pick a strong open model such as Llama, Qwen or Gemma.
2. Prepare your SFT data exactly as in Chapter 10.
3. Fine-tune with LoRA or QLoRA (LoRA on a model compressed to 4-bit) using tools like
Unsloth, Axolotl, or Hugging Face TRL with PEFT. A free Colab GPU is often enough for
models up to a few billion parameters.
4. Optionally align with preference data using DPO.
You already understand every concept involved, because you built each one.

Appendix A: Glossary
Term Plain meaning
Token A piece of text (a word, part of a word, or a
character) turned into an integer
Vocabulary The complete list of tokens the model knows
BPE Byte Pair Encoding: build tokens by repeatedly
merging the most frequent pair
Embedding A learned vector of numbers that represents a
token or a position
Parameter / weight A learned number inside the model; "11M
parameters" means 11 million of them
Context length ( block_size ) How many tokens the model can look at once
Build Your Own LLM From Scratch — A Step-by-Step Guide Book
Page 51 of 56
Term Plain meaning
Attention The mechanism that lets each token gather
information from earlier tokens
Query, Key, Value The three vectors each token makes: what it seeks,
what it offers, what it hands over
Causal mask Hides future tokens so the model cannot cheat
Head One independent attention pattern; multi-head
runs several in parallel
MLP / feed-forward The per-token network that follows attention
Residual connection Adding a layer's input to its output so signals and
gradients flow
LayerNorm Rescaling each token vector to a stable range
Logits Raw scores for every possible next token, before
softmax
Softmax Turns scores into probabilities that sum to 1
Cross-entropy loss How surprised the model is by the true next token;
lower is better
Perplexity exp(loss) : the effective number of tokens the
model is choosing between
Gradient The direction in which each parameter should
change to reduce the loss
Optimizer (AdamW) The algorithm that applies the updates
Learning rate The size of each update step
Epoch One full pass over the training data
Overfitting Memorizing the training data instead of learning
general patterns
Temperature / top-k Controls for how random generation is
Pretraining Learning language by next-token prediction on lots
of text

5. Run the pipeline, one command per cell:
!python clean.py

6. Save your work. Colab erases its files when the session ends. Copy the model to your
Google Drive:
from google.colab import drive
drive.mount("/content/drive")
!cp out/ckpt.pt data/tok.pkl /content/drive/MyDrive/
Notes: a T4 GPU does not support bfloat16, so train.py automatically runs in full
precision, which is slower but works. With only 1 MB of text, try the tiny preset first,
because the small model may start overfitting early. Kaggle notebooks work the same
way: turn on the GPU in the notebook settings and upload your files.
Appendix D: Frequently Asked Questions
Can I train on a language other than English? Yes. The tokenizer works on raw bytes, so
any script is supported. Two adjustments help: use a larger VOCAB_SIZE in prepare.py
(4,000 to 8,000), because many scripts use several bytes per character; and for scripts
that combine letters with vowel signs (such as Hindi or Bengali), change the splitting
pattern at the top of bpe.py to PAT = re.compile(r"\s?\S+|\s+") , which splits on
whitespace only. You still need enough text in that language.
Build Your Own LLM From Scratch — A Step-by-Step Guide Book
Page 55 of 56
Can I use PDFs or Word files as data? Yes, after converting them to plain text. Extract the
text with a library such as pypdf (PDF) or python-docx (Word), save it as .txt files in
raw/ , and run clean.py . Scanned PDFs need OCR first.
How do I continue training on new data? Reuse the old tokenizer and the old weights. In
prepare.py , replace the lines that create and train the tokenizer with tok =
pickle.load(open("data/tok.pkl", "rb")) . In train.py , right after model =
GPT(cfg).to(device) , add the two lines below and lower learning_rate to about 1e-4.
Copy out/ckpt.pt somewhere safe first, because training overwrites it.
start = torch.load("out/ckpt.pt", map_location=device)
model.load_state_dict(start["model"])
My model writes nonsense. What now? Check Chapter 11. The usual causes are too little
data, too few training steps, or a mismatch between the tokenizer used for training and
for sampling.
Can I use the model commercially? The model you train is yours, but the data you train on
may carry licenses or privacy limits. Check the rights to your data first (Chapter 0.12), and
ask a lawyer for anything beyond personal use.
How do I get a truly capable assistant? Apply LoRA or QLoRA to a strong open model
with your own examples (Chapter 12.4). What you learned here carries over directly.
